children.name: pinneapple_data.active_learning
children.doc:
Active Learning for adaptive collocation in PINN training.

Strategies:
- ResidualBasedAL: sample where PDE residual is highest
- VarianceBasedAL: sample where model output variance is highest (needs UQ)
- ExpectedImprovementAL: Bayesian-style expected improvement
- CombinedAL: weighted combination of strategies
- RAR (Residual-based Adaptive Refinement): the classic PINN method

classes.name: ResidualBasedAL
classes.sig: (config: ActiveLearningConfig, bounds: Dict[str, Tuple[float, float]]) -> None
classes.doc:
Sample collocation points where PDE residual is highest (RAR/RAD).

Supports two selection modes:

- ``"top_k"``: take the top-k highest residual points (RAR — Residual-based
  Adaptive Refinement).
- ``"weighted"``: sample proportional to |residual|^k, k=1 (RAD — Residual-based
  Adaptive Distribution).

Parameters
----------
config:
    :class:`ActiveLearningConfig` controlling pool size, selection count, etc.
bounds:
    Coordinate bounds ``{name: (lo, hi)}``.  The same format used by
    :class:`~pinneapple_data.collocation.CollocationSampler`.

methods.name: update_pool
methods.sig: (model = None, coord_names = None, n_candidates: Optional[int] = None) -> None
methods.doc: Refresh the candidate pool using LHS sampling from bounds.

methods.name: select
methods.sig: (residual_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], n_select: Optional[int] = None, mode: str = 'weighted') -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Select new collocation points based on PDE residuals.

classes.name: VarianceBasedAL
classes.sig: (config: ActiveLearningConfig, bounds: Dict[str, Tuple[float, float]]) -> None
classes.doc:
Sample where model output variance is highest (requires a UQ model).

This is useful when the PINN carries uncertainty estimates — e.g. a
Bayesian neural network or an ensemble — that expose a ``variance_fn``
interface.

Parameters
----------
config:
    :class:`ActiveLearningConfig`.
bounds:
    Coordinate bounds ``{name: (lo, hi)}``.

methods.name: select
methods.sig: (variance_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], n_select: Optional[int] = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Select points where output variance is highest.

classes.name: CombinedAL
classes.sig: (config: ActiveLearningConfig, bounds: Dict[str, Tuple[float, float]], residual_weight: float = 0.6, variance_weight: float = 0.3, diversity_weight: float = 0.1) -> None
classes.doc:
Weighted combination: exploit high residual + explore uncertain regions.

Scores are computed as::

    score = w_res * r̂ + w_var * v̂ + w_div * d̂

where ``r̂``, ``v̂``, ``d̂`` are normalised residual, variance, and
diversity (distance to nearest already-selected point) scores.

Parameters
----------
config:
    :class:`ActiveLearningConfig`.
bounds:
    Coordinate bounds.
residual_weight, variance_weight, diversity_weight:
    Mixing coefficients (need not sum to 1 — they are re-normalised).

methods.name: select
methods.sig: (residual_fn: Callable, variance_fn: Optional[Callable] = None, n_select: Optional[int] = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Select new collocation points via the combined score.

classes.name: AdaptiveCollocationTrainer
classes.sig: (model, physics_fn: Callable, sampler, al_config: Optional[ActiveLearningConfig] = None, optimizer = None, device: str = 'cpu') -> None
classes.doc:
Wraps a PINN model with active-learning collocation updates.

The trainer holds its own collocation set, expanding it with new points
selected by the chosen AL strategy every ``al_every`` epochs.

Usage::

    trainer = AdaptiveCollocationTrainer(
        model=pinn,
        physics_fn=burgers_loss,
        sampler=CollocationSampler.from_problem_spec(spec),
        al_config=ActiveLearningConfig(strategy="residual"),
    )
    history = trainer.train(n_epochs=2000, al_every=500)

Parameters
----------
model:
    A PyTorch ``nn.Module`` (or anything callable that takes a float32
    tensor and returns predictions).
physics_fn:
    Callable ``(model, x_col) -> (loss, residuals)`` where ``residuals``
    is a 1-D array / tensor of per-point residual magnitudes.  May also
    return just a scalar loss (in which case residuals are approximated
    via the output norm).
sampler:
    A :class:`~pinneapple_data.collocation.CollocationSampler` instance
    used to generate initial boundary/IC points.
al_config:
    :class:`ActiveLearningConfig`.
optimizer:
    Optional pre-built PyTorch optimiser.  If ``None``, Adam with
    ``lr=1e-3`` is created during :meth:`train`.
device:
    ``"cpu"`` or ``"cuda"``.

methods.name: train
methods.sig: (n_epochs: int = 2000, al_every: int = 500, n_col: int = 4096, n_bc: int = 512, lr: float = 0.001, verbose: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Train the PINN with periodic active-learning collocation refinement.

children.summary: Active Learning for adaptive collocation in PINN training.

children.name: pinneapple_data.adapters.splash_archive_adapter
children.doc:
Loader for a Splash-CFD ``.splash`` case (a zipped OpenFOAM case
directory) into plain numpy arrays -- both a flat point-cloud form (for
PINN-style training) and a dense structured-grid volume time series (for
grid-based neural operators like :class:`~pinneapple_neural.
architectures.neural_operators.fno.FNO3d`).

Promoted from the splash-pinneapple downstream project's own
``pipeline/splash_dataset.py`` / ``pipeline/splash_mesh.py`` (real,
already-used-in-production ingestion code, not a rewrite) so any project
depending on PINNeAPPle can ``pip install`` it and load a ``.splash``
archive directly -- no need to vendor this ingestion layer per-project.
Built on ``pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.binary_reader``/
``.mesh_reader`` (the real binary FoamFile / polyMesh readers) rather than
duplicating their parsing logic.

Why this is a separate adapter from
``pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.field_reader
.openfoam_case_to_upd``: that function solves a different problem -- it
reads *one* time directory from a *case directory on disk* into a single
``pinneapple_data.PhysicalSample``. This adapter reads, from a *zipped*
``.splash`` archive, several time directories at once, with
per-time-directory random subsampling, ``transportProperties``/manifest
parsing, a mesh cache to skip repeated (expensive) polyMesh
reconstruction, and (new here) reshaping into dense structured-grid
volumes for a structured single-block mesh -- none of which
``openfoam_case_to_upd`` does.

methods.doc:
Read one field (optionally one vector component) at one time
directory and reshape to a dense (nz, ny, nx) volume. Only valid
for a structured single hex block (blockMesh, x fastest / y next /
z slowest) whose cell count equals ``nx*ny*nz`` -- raises
``ValueError`` otherwise rather than silently misreshaping.

functions.name: load_mesh
functions.doc:
Build cell centers/sizes from the binary polyMesh inside a .splash
zip. ``zf`` is an open ``zipfile.ZipFile``.

functions.name: open_case
functions.doc: Open a ``.splash`` file, reconstructing (or loading a cached) mesh.

functions.name: load_dense_volumes
functions.sig: (splash_path: str, field_components: Sequence[Tuple[str, Optional[int]]], nx: int, ny: int, nz: int, *, mesh_cache_dir: Optional[str] = None) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, List[float]]
functions.doc:
Load every time directory of a ``.splash`` archive as a dense
volume time series, for a structured single hex block mesh.

Parameters
----------
field_components : e.g. ``[("U", 0), ("U", 1), ("U", 2), ("p", None)]``
    -- field name + component index (``None`` for a scalar field),
    one entry per output channel.
nx, ny, nz : the mesh's structured grid resolution. ``nx*ny*nz`` must
    equal the mesh's real cell count (checked per-field via
    ``SplashCase.read_dense_volume``, which raises rather than
    silently misreshaping a mismatched mesh).

Returns

(frames, times)
    ``frames`` : ``(T, C, nz, ny, nx)`` float32 array, ``C =
    len(field_components)``.
    ``times`` : the real simulation times, ascending, one per frame.

children.name: pinneapple_data.adaptive_sampling
children.doc:
Adaptive sampling with multiple signals: spend the evaluation budget where the model is wrong (#209).

A fixed design (Sobol', LHS) spreads the budget over the whole box. That is the right thing when nothing is known and
the wrong thing once something is: a layer, a shock, a corner or the region a surrogate has never seen carries most of
the error. This module scores a pool of candidates with several signals at once and spends the next batch on the
highest scores:

===========================  =============================================================================
``uncertainty``              the surrogate's predictive standard deviation (where it has not seen data)
``gradient``                 the magnitude of the surrogate's gradient, scaled by the box width (steep = undersampled)
``curvature``                the magnitude of the surrogate's second difference (a kink or a front)
``pde_residual``             a callable the caller gives, e.g. the residual of a PINN collocation point
``temporal_error``           a callable the caller gives, e.g. the change since the last time step of an unsteady run
``boundary_distance``        distance to the nearest face of the box: refinement where boundary layers sit
``geometry_complexity``      a callable the caller gives, e.g. distance to a wall or a surface of a CAD body
``diversity``                distance to the points already evaluated (stops the batch from collapsing on one spot)
===========================  =============================================================================

Every signal is turned into a rank (uniform on ``(0, 1)``), so no signal can dominate by its units alone, and the
score is the weighted sum. The batch is then chosen among the best 20 % of the pool by maximin distance from the
points already evaluated: the score says *where*, the distance says *not twice in the same place*. Both halves are
load-bearing: measured on the boundary layer below, with only ``boundary_distance + uncertainty`` as signals the ratio
to Sobol' is 6.9, and adding ``diversity`` to that same pair takes it to 0.39 — every candidate at the wall has the
same high score, so without the distance term the whole batch lands on one line.

:func:`adapt` is the loop, :func:`benchmark_adaptive` the documented benchmark, and the measurement is what the
promise rests on: at a budget of 64 the adaptive design cuts the surrogate's RMSE (on 4,000 held-out points) by the
factor recorded in the docstring of :func:`benchmark_adaptive`, on a smooth function it does not make it worse, and
on a feature buried in the middle of the box it does not help — the signals cannot see what the surrogate has already
smoothed away. The numbers are asserted in ``tests/test_adaptive_sampling.py``.

classes.name: GPSurrogate
classes.doc:
The default surrogate: a Gaussian process with a Matern kernel, its predictive std, and finite-difference
derivatives of its mean. Enough for the signals; any object with ``predict(X) -> (mean, std)`` can stand in.

methods.name: gradient
methods.doc: ``d y / d x`` by central differences, one step per input of ``width / 200``.

classes.name: Signal
classes.doc:
One reason to spend evaluations somewhere: a callable of ``(candidates, state) -> (n_candidates,)``, a weight,
and whether it is built from the surrogate, the caller, or the design itself.

classes.name: AdaptiveDesign
classes.doc: The evaluated points, the history of every round, and what each signal asked for.

methods.name: report
methods.doc:
What the budget bought: per round, how many points, the mean score of the batch, and the state of the
surrogate (its own RMSE on the pool is not a measurement — pass the true function to :func:`benchmark_adaptive`
for that).

functions.name: boundary_layer
functions.doc:
A layer of thickness 0.05 against the ``x1 = 0`` face: almost all of the variation sits in 5 % of the box, which
is what a fixed design undersamples. The canonical case: a wall, a shock attached to a face, a cooled edge.

functions.name: smooth
functions.doc: A low-order 2-D function with nothing localised: adaptive sampling must not be worse here.

functions.name: buried_bump
functions.doc:
A narrow Gaussian at the centre of the box, of the same scale as the layer: the case these signals do *not*
find, and the benchmark says by how much. A surrogate that has already smoothed the bump away reports neither
uncertainty nor gradient there, so the design never goes to look.

functions.name: adapt
functions.sig: (fn: Callable, space, budget: int = 64, *, n_initial: int = 16, batch: int = 8, signals: Sequence[str | Callable] = ('uncertainty', 'gradient', 'diversity'), weights: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, n_pool: int = 2000, top_fraction: float = 0.2, d_min: float | None = None, surrogate = None, seed: int = 0, initial_design: str = 'sobol') -> AdaptiveDesign
functions.doc:
Spend ``budget`` evaluations of ``fn`` on the points the signals ask for.

Parameters
----------
fn : the expensive function, ``(n, d) -> (n,)`` (a solver run, a black box, a PINN residual).
space : the box, in any of the forms :func:`_as_bounds` reads.
budget : total evaluations, ``n_initial`` of them in a space-filling design and the rest in ``batch`` rounds.
signals : names of the built-in signals (``uncertainty``, ``gradient``, ``curvature``, ``boundary_distance``,
    ``diversity``) and/or callables ``(candidates, state) -> (n_candidates,)`` and/or mappings
    ``{"pde_residual": callable, "temporal_error": callable}`` naming the signals the caller brings; ``state``
    holds ``X``, ``y``, ``mean``, ``std``, ``grad``, ``width``, ``lo``, ``hi``. Every callable is scored exactly
    like a built-in one.
surrogate : an object with ``fit(X, y)`` and ``predict(X) -> (mean, std)`` (default
    :class:`GPSurrogate`); its ``gradient(X, width)`` method, when present, feeds the ``gradient`` and
    ``curvature`` signals.
top_fraction : the batch is chosen among the best this fraction of the pool, by maximin distance from the
    points already evaluated — the score says *where*, the distance says *not twice in the same place*.
d_min : distance filter in box units used instead of the maximin pick when given (0 disables both).

The initial design is a scrambled Sobol' sequence, the same family the benchmark compares against, so the gain
comes from the scoring and not from a better start.

functions.name: benchmark_adaptive
functions.sig: (problem: str = 'boundary_layer', budget: int = 64, repeats: int = 5, n_test: int = 4000, seed: int = 0, baseline: str = 'sobol', **kw) -> dict
functions.doc:
The gain of :func:`adapt` over a fixed design at the *same* budget, on a named problem.

``baseline`` is the fixed design it is compared with: ``"sobol"`` (scrambled Sobol', the default), ``"lhs"``
(Latin hypercube) or ``"random"`` (plain uniform). On the boundary layer all three lose for the same reason —
the layer is 5 % of the box, so 5 % of the budget lands in it — and the benchmark reports each one.

For every repeat, a Sobol' design and an adaptive design of ``budget`` points are drawn, the same surrogate
(:class:`GPSurrogate`) is fitted to each, and both are scored by RMSE on ``n_test`` held-out Sobol' points of the
same box. Reported: the RMSE of both and their ratio, per repeat and as a median.

Measured on this machine (``2026-11-25``): budget 64, ``n_initial = 16``, ``batch = 8``, 6 repeats, 4,000
held-out points, signals ``uncertainty + gradient + diversity``:

===============  ==========================  ========================  ==============
problem          median RMSE, Sobol' 64       median RMSE, adaptive     median ratio
===============  ==========================  ========================  ==============
boundary_layer   2.8e-3                      1.1e-3                    0.41
smooth           7.0e-4                      4.1e-4                    0.57
buried_bump      5.6e-2                      6.4e-2                    1.14
===============  ==========================  ========================  ==============

``boundary_layer`` is the case the issue asks for: a 5 % layer against a face, where adaptive sampling is 2.5x
more accurate at the same budget. It is not a Sobol' artefact: against the other fixed designs the same run gives
a median ratio of 0.30 (LHS, worst seed 0.61) and 0.32 (uniform random, worst 0.52). Adding ``boundary_distance``
to the signals on that problem takes the Sobol' median ratio to **0.27** (worst seed 0.40) — the signal that needs
no surrogate at all is the best one there.
``buried_bump`` is the measured non-result and belongs in the documentation as much as the win: a feature the
surrogate has already smoothed away reports neither uncertainty nor gradient, so the design never goes to look
(1.14, i.e. no gain). ``smooth`` is the guard: nothing to find, no loss.

children.name: pinneapple_data.astro
pinneapple_data.astro.yt_reader
children.doc:
The output of the astrophysics codes, as ``PhysicalSample``, through `yt` (#515).

    from pinneapple_data.astro import yt_reader

    s = yt_reader.load("cosmo_sim/DD0042/output_0042")            # yt decides the format: Enzo, FLASH, GADGET ...
    s = yt_reader.load("sedov/", fields=["density", ("gas", "temperature")], level=2)
    s = yt_reader.load("snapshot_000.hdf5", to="points")          # particles stay particles
    s = yt_reader.load("output_0042", region=((0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1)))   # a box, in the dataset's units
    yt_reader.list_fields("output_0042")                          # what can be asked for, with units

`yt` (Turk et al., ApJS 2011, BSD-3-Clause) reads more than thirty formats -- Enzo, FLASH, RAMSES, GADGET, AREPO,
SWIFT, Athena/Athena++, Cholla, ART, generic HDF5 -- so one reader covers grid, AMR, particle and moving-mesh data.
It is an **optional** dependency: nothing is imported until :func:`load` or :func:`list_fields` is called, and a
machine without it gets an ImportError that says how to install it, never a broken ``import pinneapple_data``.

    pip install yt

``state`` is an ``xarray.Dataset`` on a uniform grid (``domain={"type": "grid"}``: the AMR is resampled to ``level``,
which is what a surrogate or the physics audit expects) or a dict of point arrays (``domain={"type": "points"}``:
particle data is not resampled, because the particles *are* the data). ``schema["units"]`` carries yt's units for
every field, ``provenance`` the code, the time, the box and the level, and ``extras["yt_dataset"]`` the live yt
dataset for anything this reader does not cover.

classes.name: PointState
classes.doc: The ``state`` of a points sample: a plain dict of arrays that carries the unit system it was read in.

functions.name: available
functions.doc: Whether yt can be imported, and the reason when it cannot (the sentence a caller can print).

functions.name: grid_to_dataset
functions.sig: (fields: Dict[str, Tuple[np.ndarray, str]], *, left_edge: Sequence[float], right_edge: Sequence[float], dims: Sequence[int], time: Optional[float] = None, unit_system: str = 'cgs') -> 'Any'
functions.doc:
``{name: (array, unit)}`` on a uniform grid -> ``xarray.Dataset`` with the cell centres as coordinates.

yt's grid arrays carry (x, y, z) in that order -- measured on yt 4.4.4 with a grid whose density is a function of
x alone and whose temperature is a function of z alone: ``grid[field][:, 0, 0]`` walked x and ``[0, 0, :]`` walked
z, for both ``covering_grid`` and ``arbitrary_grid``. No transpose is applied, and the test keeps it that way: a
dataset whose axes are silently transposed is a plot that looks plausible and is wrong.

functions.name: points_to_dataset
functions.sig: (fields: Dict[str, Tuple[np.ndarray, str]], *, unit_system: str = 'cgs') -> Dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Particle data as a flat ``{"x", "y", "z", <field>: values}`` dict: one row per particle, one column per field.

The ``unit_system`` is recorded on the dict's class through :class:`PointState` so the sample still says which unit
system its numbers are in after the xarray wrapper is gone (a points sample is a dict, not a Dataset).

functions.doc: Every field yt can read from this dataset, the ``(code, name)`` pairs the callers pass back.

children.name: pinneapple_data.audit
children.doc:
Physics audit of a training dataset: does the data solve its PDE? Split leakage, near duplicates, diversity and
units (#700). NumPy/SciPy only.

A model trained on wrong data inherits the error and model-level checks may never see it. Two open bugs of a widely
used library show how: generated Darcy data that did not solve the documented equation (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036) and
permeability samples with far less diversity than documented (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035). This audit checks the data
itself, before anyone trains on it.

Data layout: a split is a mapping ``{column: array}`` whose first axis is the sample (``(n,)`` for tabular columns,
``(n, ny, nx)`` for fields), as returned by ``pp.datasets.load`` or an ``.npz`` with ``<split>__<column>`` keys.

Checks (each returns pass / fail / not applicable with its evidence):

``finite``        every value finite.
``physics``       per-sample consistency with the stated PDE in the dataset's own discretisation
                  (:class:`DatasetPhysics`). Built in: ``"darcy"`` (``-div(a grad u) = f``, ``u = 0`` on the unit
                  square, cell-centred, the discretisation of ``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` and of the zoo set
                  ``darcy_2d_li2021``): the error of each stored ``u`` against the solution of the same discrete
                  problem, ``||u - A^-1 f|| / ||A^-1 f||`` (the residual measured in the ``A^-1`` norm), the boundary
                  values and the discrete flux balance. Distribution, robust outliers and the failing samples are
                  reported.
``constraints``   declared relations between columns that hold in every row (``"r_base_k_w > 0"``,
                  ``"source_width_mm == source_frac_w * base_width_mm"``).
``diversity``     effective number of distinct samples (participation ratio of the principal-component spectrum),
                  exact duplicates and near duplicates inside a split, and, when the generator is stated, the same
                  statistics and the mean radial spectrum of the inputs against freshly generated samples.
``leakage``       nearest-neighbour distance from each test sample to the training set, relative to the typical
                  distance between training samples; flagged pairs are listed.
``units``         every column with a unit in the metadata has a parseable unit, of the expected dimension when the
                  problem states one.

:func:`audit_dataset` returns an :class:`AuditCard` (JSON / markdown), :func:`audit_zoo_dataset` audits a zoo dataset
with the physics its catalog entry states.

classes.name: DatasetPhysics
classes.doc:
Per-sample physics of a dataset. ``check(sample) -> {name: relative error}`` for one sample (a mapping of
column -> array without the sample axis); ``tolerances`` maps each name to its limit (keys of
:data:`DEFAULT_TOLERANCES` or numbers).

functions.name: darcy_consistency
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Darcy sample checks in the discretisation of ``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` (cell-centred, ``h = 1/n``):
``solve`` = relative L2 distance of ``u`` to the solution of its own discrete problem; ``bc`` = RMS difference of
the boundary values (linear extrapolation of the first two cells to each face) from those of that solution, over
max |u| (the extrapolation itself is only accurate to the grid, 3.5 % of max |u| at 16 x 16 for the exact
solution, so the comparison is with the exact discrete solution, not with zero); ``flux`` = net outward boundary
flux (``2 a u`` per boundary face, the solver's own boundary flux) against the integral of ``f``.

functions.name: effective_sample_count
functions.doc:
Participation ratio ``(sum l)^2 / sum l^2`` of the principal-component spectrum of the samples (rows): about
the number of independent directions the samples span; 1 when every sample is a multiple of one pattern.

functions.name: near_duplicates
functions.doc: Exact and near duplicates inside one set (rows), relative to the median nearest-neighbour distance.

functions.name: leakage
functions.sig: (train: np.ndarray, test: np.ndarray, near: float = 0.001) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Nearest training sample of each test sample; a test sample closer than ``near`` x the median training
nearest-neighbour distance is a (near) copy.

functions.name: constraint_mask
functions.doc:
Where the declared relation ``expr`` (``"Cd > 0"``, ``"abs(u) <= 1"``, ``"a == b * c"`` to 1e-6 relative)
holds, element-wise over ``cols``: the evaluator the ``constraints`` check uses, for checking predictions too.

functions.name: audit_dataset
functions.sig: (splits: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, np.ndarray]], *, name: str = 'dataset', physics: DatasetPhysics | str | None = None, inputs: Sequence[str] | None = None, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, expected_units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, constraints: Sequence[str] = (), generator: Callable[[int, int], np.ndarray] | None = None, train: str = 'train', test: str = 'test', tolerances: Mappi...
functions.doc:
Audit ``splits`` (``{split: {column: array}}``).

``inputs``: the columns that identify a sample for diversity and leakage (default: the physics' first column,
else every numeric column). ``missing_documented``: columns whose NaN entries the metadata documents as "not
recorded". ``duplicate_splits``: the splits checked for duplicates (a grid study repeats one case on purpose). ``generator(n, seed) -> (n, ...)`` draws inputs from the stated generator (for the
diversity and spectrum comparison). ``max_physics_samples``: samples per split checked against the physics (a
random subset; ``None`` for all), since each check may solve the problem.

functions.name: audit_zoo_dataset
functions.sig: (name: str, *, offline: bool | None = None, **kw) -> AuditCard
functions.doc: Audit a ``pp.datasets`` entry with the physics and constraints its catalog entry states.

children.name: pinneapple_data.augmentation
children.doc:
Point-cloud dataset augmentation strategies for PDE/PINN training data.

Operates on the same plain `(coords, fields)` representation used throughout
this package (`coords`: (N, d) array; `fields`: {name: (N,) or (N, k) array}).
No framework/storage coupling — callers own loading and persisting datasets.

functions.name: augment_noise
functions.sig: (coords: np.ndarray, fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray], n_copies: int, std_fraction: float = 0.05, seed: int = 0) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Add Gaussian noise (scaled to each field's own std) to `n_copies`
tiled copies of the dataset. Coordinates are unchanged; only field values
are perturbed.

functions.name: augment_transform
functions.sig: (coords: np.ndarray, fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray], n_copies: int, max_rotation_deg: float = 15.0, scale_range: Tuple[float, float] = (0.9, 1.1), seed: int = 0) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Random in-plane rotation (about the first two coordinate axes) plus
isotropic scaling of the coordinate frame, `n_copies` times. Field values
are treated as physical quantities sampled at each point, not
coordinate-derived geometry — a rigid rotation/scale of the frame leaves
field *values* unchanged, so they are simply tiled to match the
(repeated) coordinate count.

functions.name: augment_interpolation
functions.sig: (coords: np.ndarray, fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray], n_new_points: int, method: str = 'linear', seed: int = 0) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Generate `n_new_points` new samples inside the convex hull of the
original point cloud, with field values estimated via scattered-data
interpolation (falling back to nearest-neighbor wherever the requested
method produces NaN, e.g. outside the interpolation method's support).

children.name: pinneapple_data.benchmark_suites
children.doc:
Public validation suites, with the dimensionless numbers their case pages publish (#171).

The regime audit answers "which bands of Reynolds and Mach does this data never reach?" on a project's own dataset.
The second half of the acceptance is the harder one: the same question asked of a **public benchmark**, where the
numbers are not ours to choose. A suite written here is only the published freestream conditions of cases whose
landing page states them, so nothing in it can be tuned to make the audit look good — and what it shows is that a
well-known reference set is missing a band that most external aerodynamics lives in.

NASA Turbulence Modeling Resource (TMR), ``https://tmbwg.github.io/turbmodels/``, read 2026-11-24. Every number below
is stated on the cited case page, and the ones the page does **not** publish are absent here rather than guessed:

========================  ========================================  ==============================  ==============
case                      Reynolds                                  Mach                            page
========================  ========================================  ==============================  ==============
2DZP flat plate          5e6 per unit length of x                  0.2 ("M = 0.2 or less")         ``flatplate_val``
2DN00 NACA 0012          6e6 per chord                             0.15 ("run M = 0.15")           ``naca0012_val``
2DBFS backward step      3.6e4 per step height, 5e3 per theta     0.128                           ``backstep_val``
2DZPH high-Mach plate    15e6 per unit length of x                 2.0 and 5.0 (three walls at 5)   ``ZPGflatplateSS_val``
ATB transonic bump       not stated                                0.875                           ``axibump_val``
ACC-SBLI Mach-7 corner   not stated                                7.11 (inflow, from 7.05)        ``axiswblim7_val``
========================  ========================================  ==============================  ==============

The Reynolds number is a function of the length it is based on, so cases based on a unit length, a chord and a step
height are kept in **separate columns**: one column with all three mixed in would answer a question about a number
that does not exist. ``reynolds`` holds only the per-unit-length-of-x values, which is the column a
``reynolds_flat_plate`` regime can read; the others are reported under their own basis.

>>> from pinneapple_data.benchmark_suites import audit_nasa_tmr          # doctest: +SKIP
>>> card = audit_nasa_tmr()                                              # doctest: +SKIP
>>> card["regime.mach"].evidence["missing"]                              # doctest: +SKIP
['subsonic']

classes.name: PublicCase
classes.doc: One published case: what its page states, and where it states it.

functions.name: nasa_tmr_cases
functions.doc: The published cases, as records (copy of the frozen tuple, for a caller that wants to filter them).

functions.name: nasa_tmr_splits
functions.doc:
The suite as an audit split: one column per basis of Reynolds, so the audit cannot compare a chord Reynolds
number with a per-unit-length one. ``reynolds`` is the flat-plate basis; ``reynolds_chord`` and
``reynolds_step_h`` carry the others.

functions.name: audit_nasa_tmr
functions.sig: (*, regimes: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = ('mach', 'reynolds_flat_plate'), name: str = 'NASA TMR validation suite') -> Any
functions.doc:
Run the dataset audit — with its regime check — on the published suite, and return the card.

The card's ``regime.*`` checks name the bands the suite never reaches; ``missing_regions()`` in their evidence is
the interval a case would have to be added in. Nothing else in the card is about regimes (the suite is a table of
published conditions, not training data), so a caller reads those checks and the audit's own findings separately.

children.name: pinneapple_data.cae
pinneapple_data.cae.compare
children.doc:
Compare two results field by field: simulation vs simulation (different meshes or models), vs experiment
(sensor tables), vs AI predictions (point tables or meshes), vs analytical or benchmark data.

The candidate is interpolated onto the reference locations (cell centres for cell fields, nodes for point fields):
directly when both use the same locations, otherwise by linear (Delaunay) interpolation inside the candidate's
domain and nearest-neighbour outside it (counted and reported). Metrics per field and per component: MAE, RMSE,
maximum absolute error and where, bias, relative L2 error, NRMSE (RMSE / reference range), R². Cell fields are
volume-weighted when cell volumes are known.

classes.name: Interpolator
classes.doc: Values of a candidate field at query points: identical locations, linear (Delaunay), nearest outside.

functions.sig: (ref: Mesh, cand: Mesh, mapping: Optional[Dict[str, str]] = None) -> List[Tuple[str, str]]

Pairs (reference field, candidate field): explicit mapping first, then same name (case-insensitive), then
aliases (U ~ velocity, p ~ pressure, T ~ temperature, DISP ~ displacement, ...).

functions.name: tolerance_verdicts
functions.doc:
Mark every field of a :func:`compare` result ``"pass"`` / ``"fail"`` by its relative L2 error against
``tolerance`` (a fraction, e.g. 0.05 for 5 %), in ``field["verdict"]``. Returns ``"PASS"`` when every judged
field passes, ``"FAIL"`` otherwise, ``None`` when nothing was judged (no tolerance or no relative error).

Abaqus / CalculiX input deck (.inp): keyword blocks, nodes, elements (to VTK types), node and element sets.

``read_deck`` keeps every keyword block with its line number, so the preflight rules can point at the line of a
problem; ``deck_mesh`` turns the deck into a ``Mesh``. *INCLUDE files are resolved from the uploaded files.

functions.doc:
The supports and loads of a deck as node ids (labels of ``*NODE``), one entry per keyword block and kind:
``*BOUNDARY`` (kind ``bc``: the constrained degrees of freedom and their values), ``*CLOAD`` / ``*CFLUX`` (kind
``load``: the sum of the nodal forces or fluxes per direction), ``*DLOAD`` / ``*DFLUX`` / ``*FILM`` on element sets or
elements (kind ``load``: the nodes of those elements, the load type and magnitude). Body loads on whole sets (GRAV,

``node_ids``, ``detail``.

children.name: pinneapple_data.cae.metrics
children.doc:
Per-cell flow metrics on a finite-volume mesh: Courant number and distance to the nearest wall.

The array functions take plain face/cell arrays (face area vectors, owner, neighbour, volumes: what
:func:`pinneapple_data.cae.geometry.face_geometry` / ``cell_geometry`` return, or what any FV code stores); the
``mesh_*`` wrappers compute those from a :class:`~pinneapple_data.cae.model.Mesh` (an OpenFOAM polyMesh read by
:func:`pinneapple_data.cae.foam.read_polymesh`, or an FE volume mesh converted to faces).

functions.name: courant_number
functions.sig: (face_area_vectors, face_owner, face_neighbour, U, cell_volumes, dt: float, where: str = 'auto') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Cell Courant number ``Co_P = 0.5 dt sum_f |U_f . S_f| / V_P`` over the faces f of cell P.

The finite-volume form of ``|U| dt / dx`` for any polyhedron (Courant, Friedrichs & Lewy, Math. Ann. 100, 1928;
Ferziger, Peric & Street, *Computational Methods for Fluid Dynamics*, 4th ed., 2020, §6.3): the outgoing plus
incoming volume flux over the cell volume, halved. On an axis-aligned hexahedron of side dx in uniform flow it
reduces to ``|U| dt / dx``.

``face_area_vectors`` (nf, 3); ``face_owner`` (nf,); ``face_neighbour`` (n_internal,) with the internal faces first
(OpenFOAM ordering). ``U`` is either a face velocity (nf, 3) or a cell velocity (n_cells, 3), interpolated to the
faces as the mean of owner and neighbour (owner value on boundary faces); ``where`` = ``"face"`` / ``"cell"``
forces the choice when the counts coincide (``"auto"`` prefers faces). Units: dt [s], U [m/s], S [m^2], V [m^3].

functions.name: wall_distance
functions.doc:
Distance from each cell centre to the nearest wall face centre (``scipy.spatial.cKDTree`` query).

With ``wall_face_normals`` (area vectors or unit normals of the same faces) the distance is projected on the
normal of that nearest face, ``|(c - f) . n|``, which is exact for a flat wall and removes the in-plane offset to
the face centre. Without normals the result over-estimates the true distance by at most half a wall face
diagonal.

functions.name: mesh_courant_number
functions.sig: (mesh: Mesh, U, dt: float, where: str = 'auto') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: :func:`courant_number` on a :class:`Mesh` (cell or face velocity ``U``, see there).

functions.sig: (mesh: Mesh, patches: Sequence[str] | None = None, project: bool = True) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
:func:`wall_distance` of every cell of a :class:`Mesh` to the faces of ``patches`` (default: every patch of
type ``wall``). ``project`` uses the face normals (see :func:`wall_distance`).

children.name: pinneapple_data.cae.repair
children.doc:
Mesh repair: turn the suggestion in ``report.ACTIONS`` into an operation, and measure the mesh before and after.

Every operation takes a :class:`~pinneapple_data.cae.model.Mesh` and returns a **new** mesh plus a
:class:`RepairResult` carrying the same metrics as :func:`~pinneapple_data.cae.quality.surface_checks` for the input
(``before``) and the output (``after``), how many faces or vertices it changed, what it guarantees and what it cannot
fix. The input mesh is never modified.

The order matters, and :func:`repair_surface` runs it:

1. :func:`merge_vertices` -- coincident vertices are welded first, because unmelted nodes are what make a surface look
   open and disconnected in the first place.
2. :func:`drop_degenerate_faces` -- a zero-area face has no normal, so it cannot be oriented or closed against.
3. :func:`drop_duplicate_faces` -- the same face twice inflates the edge count and makes an edge look non-manifold.
4. :func:`orient_consistently` -- neighbours are walked once the topology is clean, so the walk does not stop at a
   face that is about to be removed.
5. :func:`close_holes` -- holes are closed last, and each patch inherits the winding the walk just settled.

Only triangle, quad and polygon shells are repaired here. Finite-volume (polyhedral) and volume meshes are refused,
with the reason in the result: a distorted cell is a meshing decision, not a geometric edit (see #1494).

classes.name: RepairResult
classes.doc: What one operation did: the measured before and after, and an honest account of its limits.

methods.name: net_loss
methods.doc: True when the operation fixed one check by breaking another.

classes.name: RepairPlan
classes.doc: The steps of :func:`repair_surface` in the order they ran, with the consolidated before/after in ``summary``.

methods.name: no_op
methods.doc: True when every step left the mesh as it was: a clean mesh comes back unchanged and says so.

functions.name: surface_summary
functions.doc: The scalar metrics of :func:`~pinneapple_data.cae.quality.surface_checks` -- what repair measures against.

functions.name: merge_vertices
functions.doc:
Weld vertices closer than ``tol_relative * bbox diagonal`` and remap every block's connectivity.

A cluster of coincident vertices becomes one point at the cluster's mean position (so no vertex snaps onto a
neighbour's exact spot). Faces whose corners collapse onto each other are removed, and points that no block
references any more are dropped.

functions.name: drop_degenerate_faces
functions.doc:
Remove faces whose first three corners span less than ``rel_area * diagonal**2`` of area.

The threshold is the one :func:`~pinneapple_data.cae.quality.surface_checks` calls degenerate, so the before and
after counts are the same check.

functions.name: drop_duplicate_faces
functions.doc:
Remove faces that repeat a set of vertices an earlier face already used, keeping the first one.

Like :func:`~pinneapple_data.cae.quality.surface_checks`, faces are compared on their first three corners, so a
quad sharing three corners with a triangle counts as the same face.

functions.name: orient_consistently
functions.doc:
Make faces that share an edge traverse it in opposite directions, one surface shell at a time.

The walk starts at each shell's lowest-numbered face and flips only what disagrees with it. A closed shell whose
enclosed volume then comes out negative is turned inside out as a whole, so a closed surface ends with its normals
pointing outwards. Separate shells are independent: each gets its own seed and its own volume test.

functions.name: close_holes
functions.doc:
Close every boundary loop of up to ``max_edges`` edges with a fan of triangles.

A loop of up to eight edges is fanned from its highest-degree vertex, which adds no point. A longer loop gets a new
vertex at its centroid and is fanned from there, because a fan from the corner of a long loop makes long thin
triangles. Each fan walks the boundary edge the way the existing face does not, so the patch is consistent with the
surface. Loops longer than ``max_edges``, and boundary chains that do not close, are left alone and counted.

functions.name: repair_surface
functions.sig: (mesh: Mesh, rel_area: float = 1e-12, tol_relative: float = 1e-06, max_edges: int = 100) -> tuple[Mesh, RepairPlan]
functions.doc:
Run the surface pipeline in order, and report every step plus the consolidated before and after.

Returns the repaired mesh and a :class:`RepairPlan`: the list of :class:`RepairResult` in the order they ran, with
``plan.summary`` holding ``before``, ``after``, ``fixed``, ``regressed``, ``steps``, ``changed``, ``no_op`` and
``refused``. A clean mesh comes back unchanged with ``plan.no_op`` True.

children.summary: Mesh repair: turn the suggestion in report.ACTIONS into an operation, and measure the mesh before and after.

children.name: pinneapple_data.cae.xdmf
children.doc:
XDMF: read and write the mesh and the fields in one file, without loss (#115).

XDMF is an XML description of a mesh plus its data items, with the numbers either inline in the XML or in an HDF5
file next to it. It is what ParaView's "Xdmf3" reader, FEniCS and many solvers exchange, and the format a simulation
result is usually handed over in.

This module writes **XDMF3 with inline XML data** (``Format="XML"``): one file, no companion HDF5, and float64
values written with 17 significant digits, which is the round-trip precision of a double -- so a field read back is
the field written, bit for bit, and the round-trip test asserts equality rather than a tolerance. The layout is the
one ParaView and meshio understand::

    <Xdmf Version="3.0"><Domain>
      <Grid Name="pinneapple" GridType="Collection" CollectionType="Spatial">   <!-- one child per cell block -->
        <Grid Name="block0"><Topology TopologyType="Tetrahedron">...</Topology>
          <Geometry GeometryType="XYZ">...</Geometry>
          <Attribute Name="T" Center="Node" AttributeType="Scalar">...</Attribute>
          <Attribute Name="sigma" Center="Cell" AttributeType="Tensor">...</Attribute>
        </Grid>
      </Grid></Domain></Xdmf>

A mesh with one cell block is written as a plain ``<Grid>``; several blocks become the collection above, each
carrying the same geometry and its own connectivity and cell values, which is how a block-structured result stays
one file.

**Not supported, and refused with a sentence instead of half-read:**

- an XDMF whose data lives in HDF5 (``Format="HDF"`` or ``"Binary"``) -- the common ParaView output. Reading it
  needs the HDF5 companion file, which the meshio path in ``pinneapple_data.cae.io`` already handles when meshio is
  installed; this reader is for the self-contained file this module writes.
- ``Polygon``/``Polyhedron`` topologies (variable nodes per element) and time series (several ``Grid`` steps under
  one domain): neither has a place in the ``Mesh`` container, which holds one snapshot.

``MESHIO_EXT`` in ``io.py`` already lists ``.xdmf``, so an uploaded file of this kind is routed here when meshio is
absent; the two readers agree on the same block/field structure.

classes.name: XdmfError
classes.doc: A file this reader cannot read, with the reason in the message.

functions.name: write_xdmf
functions.doc:
Write a ``Mesh`` (points, cell blocks, point and cell data) as one self-contained XDMF3 file.

Raises ``XdmfError`` for what the promise does not cover: a polyhedral (OpenFOAM) mesh, a block type with no
XDMF topology, a cell field whose length does not match the mesh's cells, and a second data dimension the
attribute does not carry.

functions.name: read_xdmf

Read an XDMF3 file written with inline XML data back into a ``Mesh``.

The inverse of :func:`write_xdmf`: one cell block when the file has one ``Grid``, several when it has a
collection, with the fields at the nodes and at the cells.

children.name: pinneapple_data.chunking
children.doc: Chunking specifications and tensor iteration for streaming large arrays.

classes.name: ChunkSpec
classes.doc:
Generic chunking specification for tensors.

Backward-compatible fields:
  - mode: "none" | "time" | "spatial"  (treated as aliases for axis chunking)
  - chunk_size: chunk length along the chosen axis
  - dim: axis to chunk along (default 0)

Generic extension:
  - dims: optional multiple axes to chunk along (cartesian tiling)
  - chunk_sizes: optional per-axis chunk sizes (matches dims length)

Rules:
  - If mode == "none": yields the full tensor.
  - Else, if dims/chunk_sizes are provided: multi-axis chunking.
  - Else: single-axis chunking using dim/chunk_size.

functions.name: iter_chunks
functions.doc:
Iterate over chunks of a tensor according to a ChunkSpec.

Parameters
----------
x : torch.Tensor
    Input tensor to be chunked.
spec : ChunkSpec
    Chunking configuration describing how the tensor should be split.

Yields
------
torch.Tensor
    Sub-tensors according to the specified chunking strategy.

Behavior
--------
- If mode == "none", yields the entire tensor once.
- If dims and chunk_sizes are provided, performs recursive multi-axis
  chunking (cartesian tiling).
- Otherwise, performs single-axis chunking along `dim` using `chunk_size`.

children.summary: Chunking specifications and tensor iteration for streaming large arrays.

children.name: pinneapple_data.co_kriging
children.doc:
Co-kriging: two fidelity levels, and the discrepancy between them learned rather than assumed.

:mod:`pinneapple_data.multifidelity` answers "how much does the cheap model buy" with a closed-form kernel ridge and
a fixed relation between the fidelities. This module answers the harder question a co-kriging study asks: the cheap
model is wrong in a way that has *shape*, and the expensive runs should pay for that shape and not for the trend the
cheap model already knows.

The model is the autoregressive Kennedy-O'Hagan form::

    z_high(x) = rho * z_low(x) + delta(x)

``z_low`` is a Gaussian process over the cheap runs (``rho`` scales it to the expensive one), and ``delta`` is a
second process over what is left after the scaling -- the discrepancy. Both are fitted by maximum likelihood, the
scale ``rho`` jointly with the discrepancy's hyperparameters (see :meth:`CoKriging.fit`: estimating ``rho`` on its
own is what makes a co-kriging fit lose to a single-fidelity one). The prediction is ``rho * z_low(x) +
mu_delta(x)``, and its interval combines the two variances; the cross-covariance between ``z_low`` and ``delta`` is
not carried, so the interval is approximate and measured erratic (:meth:`CoKriging.predict` gives the numbers). The
*mean* is what this module claims.

What this buys, measured
------------------------

:func:`study` runs three models over the same expensive designs -- the cheap model alone, a single-fidelity GP on the
expensive runs, and the co-kriging model -- and scores each on held-out expensive evaluations. The claim it can
support is narrow and this module states it the way the numbers come out:

- with an expensive budget of five to twenty runs and a cheap model that is *correlated* with the expensive one, the
  co-kriging model is ahead of the single-fidelity GP by a factor this study measures per budget;
- with a cheap model that knows nothing (independent of the expensive one) it is not ahead, and the study says so
  instead of reporting the average of the two cases.

Nothing here is fitted by gradient descent: the likelihood is optimised by a bounded pattern search, so the whole
module is NumPy, and a fit is deterministic given the designs.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.co_kriging import CoKriging, study
    >>> cr = CoKriging.fit(design_low, values_low, design_high, values_high)
    >>> mean, std = cr.predict(design_test)
    >>> curve = study(forrester_low, forrester_high, budgets=(5, 10, 20))
    >>> print(curve.table())

classes.name: GaussianProcess
classes.doc:
A zero-mean Gaussian process with an RBF kernel, a noise term, and maximum-likelihood hyperparameters.

``length_scale``, ``signal`` and ``noise`` are standard deviations and a length in the *scaled* input space (the
designs divided by ``scale``), so a design in metres and one in Mach number are compared on the same footing --
the convention :mod:`pinneapple_data.multifidelity` already uses. Fitting maximises the log marginal likelihood by
a pattern search over the three logs: no gradients, no scipy, and the same answer every run.

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (x, y, *, fit_hyperparameters: bool = True, length_scale: float | None = None, signal: float | None = None, noise: float | None = None, scale = None) -> GaussianProcess
methods.doc:
Fit to ``n`` designs. With ``fit_hyperparameters=False`` the three values given are used as they are,
which is what a nested model (the discrepancy inside a co-kriging fit) wants when its samples are few.

classes.name: CoKriging
classes.doc:
Co-kriging with a discrepancy: ``z_high = rho * z_low + delta``.

``low`` is the cheap fidelity as a process over its own runs; ``discrepancy`` is fitted on
``y_high - rho * z_low(design_high)``; ``rho`` is the regression slope of the expensive values on the cheap
model's at the same designs, estimated with the means removed (so the offset the cheap model carries goes into the
discrepancy instead of being read as a scaling).

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (design_low, values_low, design_high, values_high, *, low_at_high = None, scale = None, fit_hyperparameters: bool = True, rho: float | None = None, noise_high: float | None = None) -> CoKriging
methods.doc: Fit the two levels.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: The co-kriging mean at ``design``, and its spread.

classes.name: MultiFidelityStudy
classes.doc: The three models scored on the same held-out expensive evaluations, per budget and per repeat.

methods.name: spread
methods.doc: The worst-to-best of the repeats, not a confidence interval of the median.

methods.name: better_by
methods.doc: Median error of the single-fidelity GP divided by the co-kriging one, per budget: >1 is an improvement.

methods.name: beats_single_fidelity
methods.doc: Whether two levels beat the best single level at every budget by at least ``minimum_factor``.

functions.name: forrester_high
functions.doc: The high-fidelity Forrester function: ``(6x - 2)^2 sin(12x - 4)`` on ``[0, 1]``.

functions.name: forrester_low
functions.doc:
Its cheap companion: half the expensive one plus a linear drift, so ``rho`` is not one and the discrepancy is
a line the expensive runs have to pay for.

functions.name: study
functions.sig: (low: Callable, high: Callable, *, n_low: int = 60, budgets = (5, 10, 20, 40), repeats: int = 10, seed: int = 0, bounds = ((0.0, 1.0),), test_points: int = 200, fit_hyperparameters: bool = True, spread_low: float = 1.0) -> MultiFidelityStudy
functions.doc:
Compare the cheap model, a single-fidelity GP and the co-kriging model on the same expensive budget.

``budgets`` are counts of **expensive** runs. The cheap design is ``n_low`` points drawn once from ``bounds`` and
is the same for every model and repeat -- that is what "cheap" means here, and it is why the costs are compared
on the expensive axis alone. ``spread_low`` is the standard deviation of the noise added to the *cheap* model's
values (a deterministic cheap model passes 0.0); the expensive one is treated as noiseless, because the runs a
study cannot afford twice are usually the ones with the least noise.

For each repeat the expensive designs are drawn once at the largest budget and the smaller budgets take a prefix
of them, so the comparison across budgets is nested rather than between different designs.

children.summary: Co-kriging: two fidelity levels, and the discrepancy between them learned rather than assumed.

children.name: pinneapple_data.collocation
children.doc:
Automated collocation point generation for PINN training.

Provides flexible, strategy-aware sampling from:
- Rectangular/hyperrectangular domains (from bounds or ProblemSpec)
- SDF-defined domains (from pinneapple_geom)
- Mesh-defined domains (from Mesh2D / MeshData)
- Pre-built PhysicsDomain2D objects

Sampling strategies:
- uniform   : independent uniform random
- lhs       : Latin Hypercube Sampling (better space-filling)
- sobol     : Sobol quasi-random sequence (very uniform)
- adaptive  : residual-based adaptive sampling (requires a trained model)

All outputs are numpy float32 arrays in a standard dict-batch format
compatible with the PINN training pipeline.

classes.name: CollocationConfig
classes.doc: Configuration for collocation point generation.

classes.name: CollocationSampler
classes.sig: (*, bounds: Dict[str, Tuple[float, float]], coord_names: Tuple[str, ...], sdf_fn: Optional[Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]] = None, boundary_samplers: Optional[Dict[str, Callable]] = None, condition_value_fns: Optional[Dict[str, Callable]] = None, condition_fields: Optional[Dict[str, Tuple[str, ...]]] = None, fields: Tuple[str, ...] = ('u',), strategy: str = 'lhs', seed: int = 0)
classes.doc:
Unified collocation point generator for PINN training.

Supports multiple domain sources and sampling strategies.
All outputs are in the standard pinneapple batch dict format.

Usage examples::

    # From ProblemSpec
    from pinneapple_physics.pde_environment import get_preset
    spec = get_preset("burgers_1d", nu=0.01)
    sampler = CollocationSampler.from_problem_spec(spec)
    batch = sampler.sample(n_col=4096, n_bc=512)

    # From PhysicsDomain2D
    from pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.domains import ChannelWithObstacleDomain2D
    domain = ChannelWithObstacleDomain2D(length=2.0)
    sampler = CollocationSampler.from_domain(domain)
    batch = sampler.sample(n_col=8192, n_bc_per_region=512)

    # From bounds dict
    sampler = CollocationSampler.from_bounds({"x": (0, 1), "y": (0, 1), "t": (0, 2)})
    batch = sampler.sample(n_col=4096)

methods.sig: (bounds: Dict[str, Tuple[float, float]], fields: Tuple[str, ...] = ('u',), strategy: str = 'lhs', seed: int = 0) -> 'CollocationSampler'
methods.doc: Create from explicit coord->range dict.

children.name: pinneapple_data.contracts.models
children.doc:
The four data contracts shared by the PINNeAPPle apps and the library.

=================  ===========================================================================================
``ParameterSpace``  what may vary in a study: geometry, materials, boundary conditions, operating point, with
                    bounds, units, log scaling, categories and constraints between parameters
``DatasetSpec``     a table of cases or samples on disk: columns (inputs / outputs / ids) with units, the files
                    and their SHA-256, splits, the parameter space it samples and where it came from
``ModelRef``        a trained model somewhere (zoo, file, hub): its inputs and outputs, the dataset it was
                    trained on, held-out metrics and the range it is valid in
``StudyResult``     the outcome of a study (design of experiments, campaign, UQ, sensitivity, optimisation,
                    calibration, validation): a table, metrics, the checks that ran and their records, artifacts
=================  ===========================================================================================

Every contract is a pydantic model with ``kind`` and ``schema_version`` fields, so a file says what it is::

    space = ParameterSpace(name="fin", parameters=[Parameter(name="h", low=0.01, high=0.05, unit="m")])
    space.save("fin.space.json")
    assert load("fin.space.json") == space
    ParameterSpace.json_schema()          # JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for other languages and the REST APIs

Unknown fields are refused (a typo is an error, not silently dropped); free-form additions go in ``metadata``.

Tables on disk with their contract: CSV, Parquet and HDF5, each with a JSON sidecar.

``write_table(df, "cases.parquet", contract)`` writes the table and ``cases.parquet.contract.json`` next to it.
Parquet also carries the contract in its schema metadata (key ``pinneapple.contract``) and HDF5 in a root attribute
of the same name, so the file still describes itself when the sidecar is lost. ``read_table`` returns
``(DataFrame, contract or None)``, preferring the sidecar.

children.doc:
Open data contracts shared by the PINNeAPPle apps: ``ParameterSpace``, ``DatasetSpec``, ``ModelRef``,
``StudyResult``.

Every app imports and exports these, so a design of experiments from one app is the input of a run campaign in
another, whose finished runs become a dataset for a surrogate, whose model reference goes into an uncertainty study.
JSON (or YAML) on disk, JSON Schema for other languages (``schemas/`` in this package), tables as CSV / Parquet /
HDF5 with a ``.contract.json`` sidecar::

    from pinneapple_data.contracts import Parameter, ParameterSpace, DatasetSpec, write_table, read_table

    space = ParameterSpace(name="fin", parameters=[
        Parameter(name="height", low=0.01, high=0.05, unit="m", group="geometry"),
        Parameter(name="material", kind="categorical", values=["Al6061", "Cu"], group="material")],
        constraints=["height <= 0.04 or material == 'Al6061'"])
    cases = space.from_unit([[0.5, 0.2], [0.9, 0.8]])
    cases = cases[space.feasible(cases)]

children.name: pinneapple_data.data_health
children.doc:
Engineering data health: a physics-aware quality report for sensor / test / plant data.

``load_table(bytes, filename)`` reads CSV/TSV (delimiter and decimal comma detected), Excel,
Parquet, JSON and HDF5 (1-D datasets, with ``units`` attributes when present).
``analyze(df)`` returns a JSON-ready report:

* **Units and quantities** of every column, from the header (:mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`).
* **Completeness**: missing values and long missing runs.
* **Time axis**: timestamps that go backwards, duplicates, irregular sampling, gaps.
* **Validity**: physically impossible values (below absolute zero, relative humidity above 100 %,
  pressure below vacuum), sentinel / error codes (-999, 9999, 32767...), a unit that does not fit
  the values (a "°C" column that holds kelvin) and a unit that changes mid-recording.
* **Signal quality**: stuck sensors (flat lines), spikes (Hampel filter), clipping at a range limit,
  constant columns, coarse resolution.
* **Physics consistency** (only when the columns allow it): the thermal energy balance
  Q = rho * V * cp * dT between a supply/return temperature pair, the flow and the reported
  heat rate. A flow meter that under-reads produces plausible values one column at a time; only
  the balance shows it.
* **Score**: every issue has a severity and the share of the data it affects. Each category's score
  is 100 minus its issue penalties; the overall score is the weighted mean of the categories that
  apply. The formula is returned with the report (``score.method``).

The checks are deterministic and explainable. Each issue carries its evidence (rows, time spans,
values) and a suggested fix.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets
pinneapple_data.datasets.capsule_aeroheating
children.doc:
Capsule forebody aeroheating (Bijective Systems): one wall, two fidelities, into the universal schema.

Laminar, perfect-gas heat flux and pressure on the heat shield of a parametric entry capsule. 1.024 capsules carry a
solution of an engineering model -- a modified-Newtonian panel method with Fay-Riddell stagnation heating and a Lees
laminar distribution, ``fidelity == "newtonian_panel"`` -- and 64 of them also carry a second-order laminar
Navier-Stokes solution from Eilmer, ``fidelity == "eilmer_second_order"``. Diameter runs from 0.8 m to 5.5 m, Mach
from 6 to 15 and altitude from 40 km to 80 km; the wall is isothermal at 300 K, the flow is at zero incidence, and
the gas is calorically perfect air.

Two properties of the file are what make it worth an adapter rather than a download link:

* **one wall for every capsule.** Every member's wall has 2.361 nodes and 4.640 triangles, and node *i* is the same
  point of the heat shield on every capsule and at both fidelities. The coordinates differ per capsule (metres, at
  real size); the *correspondence* does not. The difference between the two fidelities is therefore a subtraction at
  each node, with no interpolation between meshes -- which is what makes a multi-fidelity study of it meaningful,
  and is not true of any other public CFD corpus this library reads.
* **the file states its own units.** Every parameter, scalar and node field carries one (``W m-2``, ``kg m-2 s-1``,
  ``J kg-1``), and every parameter carries the bounds of its design space. Nothing here is guessed:
  :func:`schema_unit` translates the spelling, and those bounds are what :func:`field_channels` scales by.

The two fidelities are *runs*, not channels: each member is one shape at one flight condition, and the pair of runs
that share a member is what :func:`pair_fidelities` returns. Reading it the way the dataset is meant to be read:

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets import capsule_aeroheating as cap
    >>> path = cap.download("wall")                                         # 77 MB, the wall file
    >>> with cap.open_study(path) as study:
    ...     high, low = cap.pair_fidelities(study)                          # 64 rows each, same members
    ...     q_high = study.get_field("heat_flux", rows=[int(high[0])])[0]   # (2361,) W/m^2
    ...     q_low = study.get_field("heat_flux", rows=[int(low[0])])[0]     # the same nodes, the cheap model
    ...     one = cap.wall(study, int(high[0]))                             # points, triangles, every nodal field
    >>> bundle = cap.load_bundle(path, member="capsule_0066")               # one run as a PhysicsDataBundle

The cheap model is not a bad predictor: over the 64 cases its heat flux is 18.3 % off the Navier-Stokes one in
relative L2 (10.5 % to 29.7 %), its heat load 1.0 % to 15.4 % low, and its shoulder peak 11 % to 43 % low. That is
the number a surrogate trained on the expensive cases has to beat, and the reason :func:`field_samples` offers the
cheap field to the model as a channel instead of letting it meet the expensive field alone.

classes.name: Wall
classes.doc: One run's wall: the points, the triangles, and every nodal field on them.

functions.name: download
functions.sig: (what: str = 'wall', dest: str | os.PathLike[str] = 'data/capsule_aeroheating', *, revision: str | None = None, timeout: float = 600.0, force: bool = False) -> Path
functions.doc:
Fetch one of the dataset's files into ``dest`` and return its path.

``what`` is a key of :data:`FILES`. ``revision`` picks a tagged version (``"v3"``); without it the file is the
current one. A file already on disk is kept unless ``force`` is set -- these are 77 MB to 470 MB.

functions.name: open_study
functions.doc:
Open one of the dataset's ``.gamut`` files, refusing a file that is not this dataset's.

The check is on the groups and the labels the readers below rely on, not on the file name: a version of the
dataset that drops one of them should say so here rather than raise a ``KeyError`` three functions later.
Reading needs ``bijective-gamut`` (``pip install bijective-gamut``), imported here so the rest of the library
works without it.

functions.name: group_present
functions.doc: Whether a study has a group (``node_fields``, ``constants``, ...) -- the format raises when it does not.

functions.name: schema_unit
functions.doc:
The schema spelling of a unit the file reports.

Gamut writes an exponent as a trailing signed number (``W m-2``, ``kg m-2 s-1``); the schema writes it with a
caret (``W/m^2``, ``kg/(m^2*s)``). The translation is mechanical, and a spelling that still does not parse comes
back as ``"unknown"`` -- which the units gate reports -- rather than being dropped or called dimensionless.

functions.name: pair_fidelities
functions.doc:
The rows of the two fidelities, paired by member: ``(high, low)``, both sorted by member.

Every high-fidelity run has a low-fidelity run of the same member -- the cheap model runs on every capsule -- and
this pairing is what makes the difference between them a subtraction at each node. A member with no
low-fidelity run, or with two, is an error rather than something to drop: the two runs would then not be one
shape at one flight condition.

functions.name: wall
load_bundle
functions.sig: (source: str | os.PathLike[str] | Any, *, row: int | None = None, member: str | None = None, license: str = LICENSE) -> Any
functions.doc:
One run's wall as a :class:`~pinneapple_data.schema.PhysicsDataBundle`.

Give the file (or a study opened by :func:`open_study`) and either ``row`` or ``member``; with a member name and
no row, its *high-fidelity* run is the one read when it has one, and its low-fidelity run otherwise. The six
inputs go to ``physics.parameters`` with their units, the wall's isothermal temperature and the zero incidence to
``physics.boundary_conditions``, and the per-run scalars to ``metadata`` -- a bundle has a slot for parameters and
for node fields, and none for a scalar result, which is recorded rather than bent into a field.

functions.name: load_table_bundle
functions.sig: (source: str | os.PathLike[str] | Any, *, license: str = LICENSE) -> Any
functions.doc:
The run table as a bundle with no mesh: every scalar result of every run, and the six inputs.

This is the tabular-regression half of the dataset -- ``heat_load`` and the rest against the six inputs, at either
fidelity -- and the form in which the cheap and expensive runs are joined to study one against the other.

functions.name: field_pair
functions.doc:
The two fidelities of one nodal field as a :class:`~pinneapple_data.multifidelity.FieldPair`.

The expensive runs are the 64 with a Navier-Stokes solution; the cheap model's field at each of them is its own
run of the same member, so the two rows are the same wall node for node -- which is what the corpus guarantees and
what makes a field correction a subtraction. The design is the six inputs scaled by the bounds the file declares,
the same channels :func:`field_samples` offers to a model.

functions.name: field_channels
functions.sig: (study, rows: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> tuple[list[str], np.ndarray, dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
The six inputs as per-run channels, scaled to ``[-1, 1]`` by the bounds the file declares.

The bounds come from the file's own description of each parameter, so a channel is scaled by its design space
rather than by whatever the sample happened to reach. Returns the channel names, the values ``(n_rows, 6)``, and
what the scaling was -- recorded in a sample's metadata so a prediction can be mapped back.

functions.name: field_samples
functions.sig: (source: str | os.PathLike[str] | Any, *, field_name: str = 'heat_flux', fidelity: str = HIGH_FIDELITY, low_fidelity_channel: bool = True, arc_length_channel: bool = True, rows: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> list[Any]
functions.doc:
One ``FieldSample`` per run: the wall's nodes, the field on them, and what a surrogate may read besides.

A sample's ``points`` are the capsule's own wall nodes, ``values`` the requested field, ``thickness`` the arc
length from the stagnation point (the heat shield's one intrinsic coordinate), and ``extra`` the six shape and
flight inputs broadcast to every node -- followed, with ``low_fidelity_channel``, by the *cheap model's own value
of the field* on the same nodes. That last channel is the multi-fidelity part: a model that reads it predicts a
correction to the engineering model, and one built without the extra channels (``uses_extra=False``) predicts the
field from the geometry and the flight condition alone. Both are legitimate; only the first is asked to beat the
18.3 % the cheap model already reaches.

``fidelity`` selects which runs become samples -- ``HIGH_FIDELITY`` (the 64 with a Navier-Stokes solution) or
``LOW_FIDELITY`` (all 1.024). Requires ``pinneapple_arena.fieldbench`` for the sample type.

children.summary: Capsule forebody aeroheating (Bijective Systems): one wall, two fidelities, into the universal schema.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.capsule_aeroheating_physics
children.doc:
What the capsule-aeroheating dataset lets you check without trusting it: four checks, and one that checks nothing.

The reader (:mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.capsule_aeroheating`) gets the numbers out of the file. This module asks
whether they hold together, and each check here is arithmetic on the file's own arrays -- no reference solution, no
fitted parameter, nothing taken from the dataset card:

``axial_symmetry``      the flow is at zero incidence, so a field on the heat shield must be the same all the way
                        round each ring of equal arc length. This is the one check that tests the CFD data itself,
                        with no free parameter: the file states the angle of attack is zero, and a ring that disagrees
                        with itself is an error in the solution. Over the 64 CFD runs the largest within-ring spread
                        of the heat flux is 1.80 % (median 0.46 %), against the 1.20 % the dataset card reports over
                        3-80 % of the arc -- a different way of taking the ring, and the difference is stated here
                        rather than tuned away; the gate is at 2 %, which a solution that is not axisymmetric blows
                        through by an order of magnitude.
``newtonian_pressure``  the low-fidelity pressure is a modified Newtonian panel method: ``C_p = C_p,max sin^2(theta)``
                        with ``theta`` the angle between the surface normal and the freestream, and ``C_p,max`` the
                        stagnation value behind a normal shock (Rayleigh pitot). Both come from the wall's own
                        triangles and the run's own freestream, so recomputing it checks the geometry convention
                        (nodes, orientation, areas) and the units against the panel method's own output: over the
                        1.024 panel runs the median error is 0.01 % to 0.07 %, and the stagnation pressure comes back
                        to five figures. It does not check the physics: the physics question is the cheap model
                        against the CFD, which is what the dataset exists to measure (15 % median on the 64 CFD
                        runs, of which the shoulder is the largest part).
``heat_load``           the per-run scalar ``heat_load`` is the heat flux integrated over the wall. Integrating the
                        field over the triangles gives the scalar back to 0.008 % on every run.
``radiative_equilibrium``  solve ``C_H (h_r - c_p T_w) = eps sigma T_w^4`` for the wall temperature a heat shield
                        would reach. This is the *use* of the film coefficient the file carries, not a check of it.

The one thing that is **not** a check: ``q = C_H (h_r - h_w)`` holds to the last bit, because ``film_coefficient`` is
defined as ``q / (h_r - h_w)`` when the file is written. Comparing the two is an identity, and a gate built on it would
pass on any data at all -- including wrong data. It is asserted here only so that the identity is written down
somewhere rather than mistaken for a verification.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets import capsule_aeroheating as cap, capsule_aeroheating_physics as physics
    >>> with cap.open_study(path) as study:
    ...     one = cap.wall(study, int(cap.pair_fidelities(study)[0][0]))
    ...     for result in physics.checks(one):
    ...         print(result.check_id, result.status, result.value)
