classes.doc: Every number the checks produce for one run, in one place.

functions.name: cp_of
functions.doc:
The specific heat of the gas at constant pressure, J kg-1 K-1, from the study's own gamma and R.

The file states ``ratio_of_specific_heats`` and ``gas_constant`` and calls the air calorically perfect, so
``c_p = gamma R / (gamma - 1)`` is a consequence, not an assumption: 1004.675 for gamma 1.4 and R 287.05, which
is the number the dataset card quotes.

functions.name: surface_normals
functions.doc:
The outward unit normal at each node, area-weighted from the wall's triangles, ``(n_nodes, 3)``.

Area weighting is what makes a nodal normal belong to the surface rather than to whichever triangle was listed
first: a node shared by three faces is pulled towards the middle of the patch it covers.

functions.name: cell_areas
functions.doc:
The area of each face, m2, ``(n_cells,)``, by fanning it into triangles from its first node.

That is exact for a triangle and for the planar quads of the dataset's quad file. An element with a volume
(a hexahedron, a tetrahedron) has no area to report and is refused rather than answered with a number that would
be a surface of it.

functions.name: stagnation_pressure_coefficient
functions.doc:
``C_p,max``: the stagnation pressure coefficient behind a normal shock, from the Rayleigh pitot formula.

``C_p,max = 2 (p02/p_inf - 1) / (gamma M^2)``. As the Mach number grows it tends to ``2K/gamma`` with
``K = ((gamma+1)^2 / 4 gamma)^(gamma/(gamma-1)) * 2 gamma/(gamma+1)`` -- 1.839 for air, not 2: the plain
Newtonian value ``C_p = 2 sin^2(theta)`` is the limit as ``gamma`` tends to 1, and a *modified* Newtonian method
takes the stagnation value from the shock instead, which is what this dataset's panel method does.

functions.name: newtonian_pressure
functions.sig: (wall: Wall, *, coefficient: float | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray | float]
functions.doc:
The modified Newtonian pressure on every node, from the wall's triangles and the run's freestream, in Pa.

``p = p_inf + q_inf C_p,max sin^2(theta)``, with ``theta`` the angle between the outward normal and the
freestream. The freestream runs along +x with the nose at the origin (the file's own convention), so
``sin^2(theta) = n_x^2`` and the sign of the normal does not matter.

Returns the predicted pressure, the coefficient used, and ``sin^2(theta)`` per node.

functions.name: relative_error
functions.doc: ``|predicted - measured| / |measured|`` node by node, the form every check here reports.

functions.name: axial_spread
functions.sig: (wall: Wall, field: str = 'heat_flux', *, atol: float = 1e-09) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
``std/mean`` of a field within each ring of equal arc length, and the rings themselves.

Nodes whose arc length from the stagnation point agrees to ``atol`` metres belong to the same ring: the wall is
revolved, so they are the same station of the heat shield at different angles round the axis. Rings with fewer
than three nodes are left out -- a "ring" of two points has no spread worth reporting.

The rings are taken from the ``arc_length`` field the file carries, not reconstructed from the geometry, so this
is the dataset's own station numbering. The dataset card reports a spread "from the median at their distance from
the stagnation point" over 3-80 % of the arc; this measure uses the ring's mean over every ring, which comes out
slightly larger at the extremes (see the module docstring).

functions.name: heat_load
functions.doc:
The field integrated over the wall: per triangle, the mean of its three nodal values times its area.

The scalar ``heat_load`` the file reports is this integral at the run's flight condition. The integration is the
plain one a nodal field admits (mean of the corners, not a quadrature with a shape function), which on this wall
reproduces the reported scalar to a few hundredths of a per cent -- so the tolerance below is set for that and not
for a method that cannot do better.

functions.name: wall_heat_flux
functions.doc:
``q(T_w) = C_H (h_r - c_p T_w)``: the heating on a wall held at ``temperature``, W m-2.

What the file's 300 K wall gives at another temperature, holding the film coefficient at its 300 K value -- which
the card says runs a few per cent high on a hot wall, because ``C_H`` falls a little as the wall heats.

functions.name: radiative_equilibrium_temperature
functions.sig: (wall: Wall, *, emissivity: float = 0.85, iterations: int = 100) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
The wall temperature at which radiation carries away all the heating, per node, K.

Solves ``C_H (h_r - c_p T) = eps sigma T^4`` by bisection between the wall's own temperature and the adiabatic
wall temperature ``h_r / c_p``: the left side falls with ``T`` and the right side rises, so the root is bracketed
and single. ``emissivity`` is the caller's choice -- the file states none -- and is the one number in this module
that is not the dataset's own.

Where the node is being *cooled* by the flow (``C_H (h_r - c_p T_w) <= 0``, which the film coefficient of this
dataset is not), there is no heating to radiate and the answer is the wall temperature itself.

functions.name: closure_identity_residual
functions.doc:
The largest relative gap in ``q = C_H (h_r - h_w)`` -- which is zero, and is not a check.

``film_coefficient`` is defined as ``q / (h_r - h_w)`` when the file is written, so this residual is a property of
the arithmetic, not of the data. It is here so the identity is on the record and nobody mistakes it for a
verification: a gate built on it passes on garbage.

functions.name: checks
functions.sig: (wall: Wall, *, emissivity: float = 0.85, pressure_tolerance: float = 0.01, symmetry_tolerance: float = 0.02, heat_load_tolerance: float = 0.001) -> list
functions.doc:
The four checks as :class:`~pinneapple_data.schema.models.CheckResult`, for the bundle's ``verification``.

A check that the run cannot answer is recorded as not run (``passed=None``) rather than passed: the Newtonian
pressure is only the panel method's own value on a ``newtonian_panel`` run, and on an ``eilmer_second_order`` run
the same comparison measures the cheap model against the CFD, which is a different question and is reported as
such in the detail rather than as a pass.

functions.name: record
functions.doc:
Write the checks into a bundle's manifest, so the record travels with the data.

``required=True`` makes them part of what the bundle claims to have passed: :attr:`Verification.passed` then needs
every one of them to have run and passed, and a check left unrun keeps the bundle from claiming a verdict.

functions.name: summary
functions.doc: The same numbers as :func:`checks`, as one dataclass -- for a table across runs.

children.summary: What the capsule-aeroheating dataset lets you check without trusting it: four checks, and one that checks nothing.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.catalog
children.doc:
The dataset catalogue: what external physics data exists, how it is reached, and what reading it takes.

The registry in :mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.registry` answers "which arrays can I get in this process" -- it is
a name to loader table. This module answers the question a person actually asks first: *which public dataset
covers this physics, in what format, under what licence, and is there an adapter here that reads it?*

Two fields carry the honesty of the catalogue:

* ``adapter`` -- ``None`` where this library has no reader. The entry then names the formats and the homepage, so
  the next step is a decision, not a discovery. A catalogue that listed ten datasets with no way to tell which
  ones work is a reading list, not an integration;
* ``license`` + ``license_verified`` -- a licence read off the project's own distribution page is marked verified;
  anything taken from memory or from a repository's ``LICENSE`` file without checking which artefact it covers is
  marked unverified, because "the code is MIT" says nothing about the 15 TB of data beside it.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.catalog import CATALOG, entries, implemented
    >>> [e.id for e in entries(priority="P0")]
    ['cfdbench', 'nasa_tmr', 'pdebench', 'spe10', 'the_well']
    >>> [e.id for e in implemented()]           # the ones with a working reader in this library
    ['cfdbench', 'flowbench', 'pdebench', 'spe10', 'the_well']

classes.name: CatalogEntry
classes.doc: One external dataset: where it is, what it holds, what it may be used for, and what reads it.

methods.name: readable
methods.doc: Whether this library can turn the dataset into a bundle today.

functions.name: entries
functions.sig: (*, priority: str | None = None, domain: str | None = None, readable: bool | None = None, stage: str | None = None) -> list[CatalogEntry]
functions.doc:
The catalogue, filtered and sorted by priority then id.

``stage=`` filters on the workflow stages an entry feeds (``CatalogEntry.stages``, the ids of
:mod:`pinneapple_catalog.stages`): "which public data can I get for the inverse step" is a question the
catalogue could not answer while it was organised only by priority and domain.

functions.name: implemented
functions.doc: The catalogued datasets this library can actually read into a bundle today.

functions.name: missing
functions.doc: The catalogued datasets with no reader here -- the backlog, written down.

functions.name: redistributable
functions.doc:
Whether the dataset's licence is *known* to allow redistribution.

``False`` is not a legal opinion: it means the licence has not been verified here, which is the only safe
answer to give before someone ships the data inside a product. ``True`` is not a commercial clearance either:
a non-commercial licence (FlowBench's CC-BY-NC-4.0) grants redistribution and still forbids the product, so the
entry's ``license`` text is what the decision is made on.

functions.name: to_json
functions.doc: The catalogue as JSON-ready dicts (the payload the Engineering API serves).

children.summary: The dataset catalogue: what external physics data exists, how it is reached, and what reading it takes.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.cfdbench
children.doc:
CFDBench: the 2-D incompressible cases, as written on HuggingFace, into the universal schema.

CFDBench (Luo, Chen & Zhang, 2023; arXiv:2310.05963) is four families of incompressible flow -- lid-driven
``cavity``, flow through a ``tube``, flow over a ``dam`` and flow around a ``cylinder`` -- each with three subsets that
vary the boundary conditions (``bc``), the geometry (``geo``) or the fluid properties (``prop``). The archive on
HuggingFace published the fields interpolated to a 64 x 64 grid, which is the form every paper on it uses.

The layout is the project's own, read from its loader (``src/dataset/base.py`` and ``src/dataset/*.py``) rather than
guessed:

    cavity/bc/case0000/u.npy      # (time, height, width), float
    cavity/bc/case0000/v.npy      # (time, height, width)
    cavity/bc/case0000/mask.npy   # (height, width), 1 on the boundary and 0 in the interior -- where it exists
    cavity/bc/case0000/case.json  # the case's parameters (viscosity, density, boundary speeds, geometry extents)

Two things this reader refuses to invent:

* **the units.** Neither the archive nor ``case.json`` states them, so every field is ``unknown`` unless the caller
  passes ``units={...}``. That is a verdict the ``units`` gate reports, not a conversion decided here.
* **the coordinates.** The interpolated grid carries no coordinate arrays. Where ``case.json`` gives the domain's
  extent (the cylinder family gives ``x_min``/``x_max``/``y_min``/``y_max``) the cell centres are built from it and
  the length unit is still ``unknown``; where it does not, the axis is the cell index and dimensionless. Both cases
  say which one they are in the bundle's metadata.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets import cfdbench
    >>> case = next(cfdbench.open_cases("data/CFDBench", problem="cavity"))
    >>> bundle = cfdbench.load_bundle(case, dt=0.1)          # the cavity's frames are 0.1 s apart

classes.name: Case
classes.doc: One case on disk: its fields, its mask and the parameters ``case.json`` records.

methods.name: arrays
methods.doc: ``u``, ``v`` and, where the case ships one, ``mask`` -- loaded here, not at construction.

methods.name: params
methods.doc: The numeric parameters of ``case.json``; a key that is not a number is left to the raw metadata.

functions.name: open_cases
functions.sig: (root: str | os.PathLike[str], *, problem: str | None = None, subset: str | None = None) -> Iterator[Case]
functions.doc:
Every case under ``root``, sorted: ``root/<problem>/<subset>/caseNNNN``, or ``root/<subset>/caseNNNN`` when
``root`` is one unpacked problem -- which is how the archives extract (``tube.zip`` unpacks to ``bc/``, ``geo/``,
``prop/`` at the top level, with no ``tube/`` above them).

functions.name: load_bundle
functions.sig: (case: Case | str | os.PathLike[str], *, license: str = LICENSE, dt: float | None = None, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, source: str = '') -> Any
functions.doc:
One case as a bundle: ``u``/``v`` as a velocity vector, the mask as a field, ``case.json`` as parameters.

``dt`` (seconds per frame) turns the frame index into a time axis; without it the axis is the index. The cavity
family's frames are 0.1 s apart, which the project's loader states and this module does not assume.

functions.name: download
functions.sig: (problem: str, root: str | os.PathLike[str] = 'data/cfdbench', *, timeout: float = 600.0) -> Path
functions.doc:
Fetch and unzip one problem's archive into ``root``; returns the directory the cases are under.

The files are on HuggingFace (``cavity.zip``, ``dam.zip``, ``tube.zip`` and three zips for ``cylinder``); this
downloads them whole, because they are zips -- the range-request reader exists for datasets that are one big
HDF5 file, not for an archive that has to be unpacked anyway.

children.summary: CFDBench: the 2-D incompressible cases, as written on HuggingFace, into the universal schema.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.deepmind_mgn
children.doc:
DeepMind ``meshgraphnets`` datasets: partial download, TFRecord reader and conversion to tensors.

The datasets of Pfaff et al., "Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks", ICLR 2021
(``cylinder_flow``, ``airfoil``, ``flag_simple``, ...), are published as one ``meta.json`` plus one TFRecord file per
split under https://storage.googleapis.com/dm-meshgraphnets/<dataset>/. Reading the records needs
``pip install tfrecord`` (no TensorFlow).

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.deepmind_mgn import download_prefix, read_trajectories
    >>> download_prefix("cylinder_flow", "valid", Path("data/cylinder_flow"), nbytes=50_000_000)  # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> trajs = read_trajectories(Path("data/cylinder_flow"), "valid", max_traj=4)              # doctest: +SKIP

functions.name: download_prefix
functions.sig: (dataset: str, split: str, dest: Path, nbytes: int) -> Path
functions.doc:
Download ``meta.json`` and the first ``nbytes`` of ``<split>.tfrecord`` of a DeepMind dataset into ``dest``.

TFRecord is a sequential format, so a byte prefix holds whole leading trajectories (the truncated last record is
dropped by :func:`read_trajectories`). Files already present are not downloaded again. Returns the record path.

functions.name: read_trajectories
functions.sig: (data_dir: Path, split: str, max_traj: int) -> list[dict[str, np.ndarray]]
functions.doc:
Read up to ``max_traj`` trajectories of ``<data_dir>/<split>.tfrecord`` as dicts of numpy arrays.

Field shapes follow ``meta.json``: static fields (``mesh_pos``, ``cells``, ``node_type``) lose the leading time
axis, dynamic ones (``velocity``, ``pressure``, ...) are ``(T, N, C)``. A truncated last record (prefix download)
ends the read.

functions.name: cylinder_flow_to_tensors
functions.sig: (traj: dict[str, np.ndarray], node_type_map: dict[int, int] = CYLINDER_TYPE_MAP) -> tuple[MeshGraph, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]
functions.doc:
``cylinder_flow`` trajectory -> ``(MeshGraph, velocity (T, N, 2), pressure (T, N, 1))``.

``node_type_map`` collapses the raw ids to contiguous classes (default :data:`CYLINDER_TYPE_MAP`).

children.summary: DeepMind meshgraphnets datasets: partial download, TFRecord reader and conversion to tensors.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.download
children.doc:
Download a URL once into a local cache, with retries (standard library only).

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.download import fetch_cached
    >>> path = fetch_cached("https://example.org/catalog.csv", "data/.cache")
    >>> text = path.read_text()

The cache file is named after the MD5 hash of the URL (plus the URL's file extension), so the same URL is fetched
once and different URLs never collide. The body is written to a temporary file and renamed when complete: an
interrupted download never leaves a truncated file that a later call would mistake for a cached one.

functions.name: cache_path
functions.doc: The file :func:`fetch_cached` uses for ``url``: ``<cache_dir>/<md5(url)><ext>``.

functions.name: fetch_cached
functions.sig: (url: str, cache_dir: str | Path, *, tries: int = 4, timeout: float = 60, backoff: float = 2.0) -> Path
functions.doc:
Return a local copy of ``url``, downloading it only if it is not cached yet.

Parameters
----------
url : any URL ``urllib.request.urlopen`` accepts (``https://``, ``http://``, ``file://``).
cache_dir : directory of the cache (created if missing).
tries : number of attempts before giving up.
timeout : socket timeout per attempt, in seconds.
backoff : the wait before attempt ``k + 1`` (``k = 1, 2, ...``) is ``backoff ** (k - 1)`` seconds
    (1, 2, 4, ... for the default), i.e. exponential backoff.

Returns
-------
Path of the cached file.

Raises
------
RuntimeError if every attempt fails (the last error is chained).

children.summary: Download a URL once into a local cache, with retries (standard library only).

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.external_sources
children.doc:
External data source integrations for PINNeAPPle.

Provides loaders for 15 scientific/engineering data sources with automatic
fallback to cached or synthetic data when the source is unavailable.

Sources
-------
  materials_project   — Crystal structures, electronic/thermal properties (mp-api)
  nomad               — Ab-initio / DFT calculations (NOMAD REST API)
  nasa_open_data      — CFD, exoplanet, climate datasets (data.nasa.gov)
  noaa                — Ocean / atmosphere / climate data (NOAA ERDDAP / NCEI)
  copernicus          — Sentinel, atmosphere, ocean (CDS API)
  brazil_data_cube    — Satellite time series for Brazil (STAC API)
  cptec_inpe          — Numerical weather prediction (CPTEC/INPE)
  ons                 — Brazilian power grid data (dados.ons.org.br)
  nrel                — Solar / wind / energy systems (NREL API)
  designsafe          — Earthquake / structural / FEM data (DesignSafe API)
  openfoam_tutorials  — CFD cases from OpenFOAM tutorial collection
  su2                 — Aerodynamics / CFD / optimization (SU2 Foundation)
  nasa_power          — Daily point meteorology / solar resource (NASAPowerClient)
  open_meteo          — Hourly historical weather archive (OpenMeteoClient)
  destine             — Destination Earth platform: the Digital Twin catalogue and the
                        Climate DT collections (DestinEClient)

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_data.datasets import load_dataset

    # Basic load — returns Dict[str, np.ndarray]
    data = load_dataset("materials_project_band_gap")
    data = load_dataset("noaa_ocean_temperature")
    data = load_dataset("openfoam_cylinder_drag")

    # Source-specific clients for richer queries
    from pinneapple_data.datasets.external_sources import MaterialsProjectClient
    client = MaterialsProjectClient(api_key="YOUR_KEY")
    docs = client.query({"band_gap": {"$gt": 1.0}}, fields=["band_gap", "structure"])

Authentication
--------------
  Materials Project : MP_API_KEY environment variable or api_key param
  NREL              : NREL_API_KEY environment variable or api_key param
  Copernicus CDS    : ~/.cdsapirc config file (see https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu)
  DestinE           : DESTINE_CLIENT_ID / DESTINE_CLIENT_SECRET (service account key) for items
                      and downloads; the catalogue itself needs no credentials
  All others        : public REST APIs, no key required

classes.doc:
Client for the NASA POWER daily point API (meteorology and solar resource, no API key).

Docs: https://power.larc.nasa.gov/docs/services/api/temporal/daily/ . Network errors and HTTP errors raise.

    >>> c = NASAPowerClient()
    >>> js = c.fetch_daily(latitude=-8.05, longitude=-34.9, start="20240101", end="20240131",
    ...                    parameters=["T2M", "PRECTOTCORR"])                         # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> arrays = c.to_arrays(js)          # {"date": datetime64[D], "T2M": ..., "PRECTOTCORR": ...}  # doctest: +SKIP

methods.name: fetch_daily
methods.sig: (*, latitude: float, longitude: float, start: str, end: str, parameters: list[str], community: str = 'SB', time_standard: str = 'UTC', timeout: int = 60) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Raw JSON of daily ``parameters`` at one point; ``start``/``end`` as ``"YYYYMMDD"``.

methods.name: to_arrays
methods.doc:
``{"date": datetime64[D] (T,), <PARAM>: float64 (T,)}``; the POWER fill value (``header.fill_value``,
-999) and missing days become NaN. Dates are the sorted union over all parameters.

methods.name: to_physical_samples
methods.doc:
One :class:`pinneapple_data.physical_sample.PhysicalSample` with ``state["x"]`` ``(T, D)`` float32 (columns
= sorted parameter names), ``state["t"]`` ``(T, 1)`` day index, provenance from the response header.

classes.name: OpenMeteoClient
classes.doc:
Client for the Open-Meteo Historical Weather API (ERA5-based reanalysis, hourly, no API key; CC BY 4.0).

Docs: https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api . Network errors and HTTP errors raise.

    >>> d = OpenMeteoClient().fetch_archive(-5.795, -35.209, "2026-08-01", "2026-08-30",
    ...                                     hourly=["temperature_2m", "shortwave_radiation"])  # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> d["time"][:2], d["temperature_2m"][:2]                                                  # doctest: +SKIP

methods.name: fetch_archive_json
methods.sig: (latitude: float, longitude: float, start_date: str, end_date: str, hourly: list[str], *, timezone: str = 'UTC', temperature_unit: str = 'celsius', wind_speed_unit: str = 'kmh', precipitation_unit: str = 'mm', timeout: int = 60) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Raw JSON of the ``hourly`` variables between ``start_date`` and ``end_date`` (``"YYYY-MM-DD"``).

methods.name: hourly_arrays
methods.doc:
``{"time": datetime64[m] (T,), <variable>: float64 (T,)}`` from an archive response (null -> NaN).
Times are local to the requested ``timezone``.

methods.name: fetch_archive
methods.sig: (latitude: float, longitude: float, start_date: str, end_date: str, hourly: list[str], **kwargs) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
methods.doc: :meth:`fetch_archive_json` followed by :meth:`hourly_arrays`.

classes.name: DestinEClient
classes.sig: (client_id: str | None = None, client_secret: str | None = None, token: str | None = None, timeout: int = 60) -> None
classes.doc:
Client for the DestinE Platform (Destination Earth, EU) and its Data Lake.

The platform has two tiers, and the difference decides what a caller can do:

* **Discovery, no credentials.** :meth:`collections` lists the whole portfolio (348
  collections when checked in 2026-11, of which 72 are Climate DT and 2 Extremes DT) and
  :meth:`collection` / :meth:`variables` read one collection's metadata: variables with
  units, dimensions, temporal extent, licence and DOI.
* **Items and assets, OAuth2 token.** :meth:`search`, :meth:`items` and :meth:`download`
  send a bearer token from the ``client_credentials`` grant of the platform's Keycloak
  realm. The Digital Twins collections (the ``DT_CLIMATE`` and ``DT_EXTREMES`` ones) need
  more than a token: the platform gates them behind an *upgraded access* that is requested
  per user, so they answer 403 until it is granted.

Keep the two apart: a catalogue of what exists is available to anyone, and the km-scale
fields are not. A 403 here is that gate, not a bug.

Docs: https://platform.destine.eu/ . Registration (free) makes the account; the key pair
comes from a service account in My DataLake Services and is read from
``DESTINE_CLIENT_ID`` / ``DESTINE_CLIENT_SECRET`` (or passed in). Errors that are not a
refusal (401/403) propagate as :class:`urllib.error.HTTPError`.

    >>> c = DestinEClient()
    >>> dt = c.climate_dt_collections()                     # no token, no account  # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> dt[0]["id"]                                                                  # doctest: +SKIP
    'EO.ECMWF.DAT.D1.DT_CLIMATE.G1.CMIP6_HIST_ICON.R1'
    >>> vars = c.variables(dt[0]["id"])                                              # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> vars["Temperature(clte_pl)"]["unit"]                                         # doctest: +SKIP
    'K'
    >>> c.search(dt[0]["id"], bbox=(-44, -24, -42, -22), limit=5)                     # doctest: +SKIP
    Traceback (most recent call last):                        # without a token or with the
    PermissionError: DestinE: ...                             # gate closed: 401 / 403

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.flowbench
children.doc:
FlowBench: flow over complex geometries, from the tensors the archive publishes.

FlowBench (Tali et al., 2024, arXiv:2409.18032) is the benchmark for neural simulators on **complex geometries**: a
shifted-boundary-method solver run over thousands of shapes, published on HuggingFace as ``BGLab/FlowBench``. This
module reads the two shapes the archive actually stores, both checked against the files themselves:

``X``/``Y`` tensors (the LDC families)
    one ``.npz`` per family, resolution and geometry family -- ``LDC_NS_2D/128x128/harmonics_lid_driven_cavity_X.npz``
    -- holding a single dataset ``data`` shaped ``(n_samples, n_channels, height, width)``. The channel lists are
    Table 12 of the paper: ``X`` is ``[Re, g, s]`` (or ``[Re, Gr, g, s]`` for the heat-transfer families) and ``Y`` is
    ``[u, v, p]`` (or ``[u, v, p, theta]``). Measured on the published 128 x 128 file: ``X`` is ``(1000, 3, 128,
    128)``, ``Y`` is ``(1000, 4, 128, 128)``. Channel names are assigned **by their count**, so a file whose counts
    match no documented row is refused instead of silently mislabelled -- the 128 x 128 file above, for instance, has
    the 3-channel input of the Navier-Stokes family and the 4-channel output of the heat-transfer one, and says so in
    the bundle's metadata rather than picking a story.

``FPO`` per-sample files
    ``FPO_NS_2D_1024x256/<geometry family>/<case>/Re_<value>.npz`` holds ``data`` shaped ``(n_time, height, width,
    channels)`` -- measured ``(242, 256, 1024, 3)`` -- with ``u, v, p`` **last**; the companion ``input_geometry.npz``
    holds ``data`` (a distance field) and ``mask`` (1 inside the solid). These files are 1.4 GB each, which is why the
    reader takes a path or a URL and reads one file, not a family.

The licence is CC-BY-NC-4.0 -- stated on the dataset card and in the paper ("Our datasets and code are licensed under
CC-BY-NC-4.0"), so it is recorded as verified, and it is **non-commercial**: `redistributable` in the catalogue says
the licence was checked, not that the data may ship in a product.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets import flowbench
    >>> bundle = flowbench.load_tensors(".../LDC_NS_2D/128x128/harmonics_lid_driven_cavity_X.npz",
    ...                                 ".../harmonics_lid_driven_cavity_Y.npz", index=0)  # doctest: +SKIP

1024, 3)`` -- not second as in the ``X``/``Y`` tensors.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.operator
children.doc:
A dataset in the shape an operator model learns from: ``initial condition -> trajectory``.

An operator (FNO, DeepONet, U-NO) learns a map between *functions*, not between points. A PDEBench file or a set of
bundles holds trajectories; the adapter here turns them into the two tensors that map is trained on:

* ``inputs["ic"]`` -- the first snapshot of each trajectory, ``(N, X)``;
* ``inputs["params"]`` -- the scalar parameters that differ between trajectories (Reynolds, viscosity, beta), when
  the source records them, ``(N, P)``;
* ``targets`` -- the whole trajectory, ``(N, T, X)``.

The split is by **trajectory**, never by sample point: splitting a trajectory's own time steps between train and
test measures interpolation, which an operator that has seen the trajectory will pass and a new initial condition
will not. :meth:`OperatorDataset.leakage` checks exactly that, and the report says so.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.operator import from_pdebench
    >>> op = from_pdebench("https://darus.../1D_Burgers_Sols_Nu0.001.hdf5", samples=range(64), field="u")
    >>> op.split(0.7, 0.15).test.targets.shape
    (10, 201, 1024)
    >>> op.channels(index=0).shape            # what an FNO takes: (C, X) with the IC and any parameters
    (1, 1024)

Reading 64 trajectories over range requests is 64 reads; a local file is the better choice for a real training run
(:func:`pinneapple_data.datasets.pdebench.download`).

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.pdebench
children.doc:
PDEBench: read its HDF5 files into the universal schema, locally or straight off the archive.

PDEBench (Takamoto et al., NeurIPS 2022, "PDEBench: An Extensive Benchmark for Scientific Machine Learning";
data DOI `10.18419/darus-2986 <https://doi.org/10.18419/darus-2986>`_, CC BY 4.0) ships the reference PDE datasets
that almost every operator-learning paper reports on. This module reads them without a full download:
:mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.remote_hdf5` serves the HDF5 metadata and only the chunks a sample touches, so the
one sample a benchmark needs costs megabytes, not the 1.3-88 GB of the file it lives in.

Two layouts, both of which appear in the archive
------------------------------------------------
``tensor``
    root datasets only: one or more fields shaped ``(n_samples, n_time, *spatial)`` -- or ``(n_time, *spatial)``
    when the file holds a single trajectory -- plus ``x-coordinate`` / ``y-coordinate`` / ``z-coordinate`` /
    ``t-coordinate`` and, for the parametric families, a per-sample parameter array (``nu``, ``beta``, ``M``,
    ``eta``...). ``Sod6.hdf5`` and the ``*_Sols_*`` files are this layout, and it is the one verified against the
    published files in the tests.
``groups``
    one group per sample (``0000``, ``0001``, ...), each holding its fields and coordinates. This is the layout
    the paper's own ``data_gen`` writes; the reader follows the layout as documented and is exercised on a
    reproduction of it in the tests, not on a downloaded multi-gigabyte file.

What is preserved, and what is not
----------------------------------
* field names are canonicalised (``density``, ``pressure``, ``velocity`` with components ``u``/``v``/``w``,
  ``Vx``/``Vy``/``Vz`` folded into ``velocity``) and the raw names stay in ``metadata["pdebench"]["raw_fields"]``,
  so nothing is lost by the renaming;
* every value is dimensionless in the archive's own non-dimensionalisation, and the schema records ``"1"`` rather
  than inventing SI units;
* coordinates are read from the file, never assumed -- and where a coordinate array disagrees with the data it
  indexes (``Sod6.hdf5`` carries 202 time coordinates for 201 snapshots), the adapter aligns the shorter of the two
  and records the discrepancy in ``metadata["pdebench"]["notes"]`` and in a ``time_alignment`` check. That
  disagreement is exactly the kind of thing a silent reader hides.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.pdebench import load_bundle
    >>> bundle = load_bundle("https://darus.uni-stuttgart.de/api/access/datafile/133150")   # Sod6, 4.9 MB
    >>> bundle.manifest.fields.names()
    ['density', 'pressure', 'velocity']

classes.doc:
What equation a family solves, in words and symbols -- the ``Physics`` a bundle is stamped with.

classes.name: PDEBenchFile
classes.sig: (source: str | Path | Any, *, handle: Any = None, keep_open: bool = True, **open_kwargs) -> None
classes.doc:
An open PDEBench HDF5 file: metadata now, samples on demand.

Use :func:`open_pdebench` (a context manager) rather than constructing this directly, unless you already hold
an open ``h5py.File``.

The reader classifies the leading axes of the file before it reads anything: whether the leading axis is a
*sample* axis, a *time* axis or a *component* axis is not written anywhere in the file, and getting it wrong
turns a (10000, 201, 1024) dataset into 10000 samples of 201 points -- the kind of mistake that looks like a
working pipeline. The classification is arithmetic on the coordinate lengths vs the dataset shape, and the
outcome is kept in :attr:`axis_flags` where a caller can see and disagree with it.

children.doc:
Pre-built physics datasets for PINNeAPPle benchmarks.

All datasets are generated analytically or via scipy method-of-lines.
No external data files required — everything is reproducible from code.

functions.name: burgers_periodic_solve
functions.sig: (u0: np.ndarray, T: float, nu: float, *, length: float = 1.0, refine: int | None = None, cfl: float = 0.5) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Solve periodic viscous Burgers ``u_t + (u^2/2)_x = nu u_xx`` from ``u0`` (``(..., nx)``) to time ``T``.

Fourier pseudo-spectral in space with 2/3-rule dealiasing (Orszag 1971), integrating-factor fourth-order
Runge-Kutta in time (the diffusion is integrated exactly; Kassam & Trefethen, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 26, 2005,
sec. 2). ``u0`` is sampled at ``x_j = j length / nx``. The solve runs on ``refine`` times more points (the
initial condition is Fourier-interpolated) and is sampled back on the input grid; ``refine=None`` picks the
smallest power of two (at most 16) with cell Reynolds number ``max|u0| dx / nu <= 1``, so viscous shocks are
resolved. The time step is ``cfl * dx / max|u0|`` (``max|u|`` does not grow: maximum principle).
Returns ``u(x_j, T)`` (float64, same shape as ``u0``).

functions.name: burgers_periodic_pairs
functions.sig: (n: int, nx: int = 128, T: float = 1.0, nu: float = 0.01, seed: int = 0, *, length: float = 1.0, refine: int | None = None)
functions.doc:
``n`` random pairs ``(u(x, 0), u(x, T))`` of periodic viscous Burgers on ``[0, length)`` (operator learning).

Initial conditions: ``sum_{k=1..K} a_k sin(2 pi k x / length + phi_k)`` with ``K ~ U{3..7}``,
``a_k ~ U(-1, 1)``, ``phi_k ~ U(0, 2 pi)``; solved by :func:`burgers_periodic_solve`.
Returns ``(x (nx,), u0 (n, nx), uT (n, nx))`` as float32, ``x_j = j length / nx``.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.read
children.doc:
Choosing a catalogued public dataset and reading it — the dispatch behind the stage map's data half.

The catalogue answers "which archives exist and which have a reader". This module answers the next two questions a
pipeline asks: **which one should I use for this stage**, and **how do I actually get a bundle out of it**.

The choice is deterministic and its rule is written down, because a recommender whose rule is hidden cannot be
argued with:

1. the dataset must be tagged with the stage;
2. with ``bundle_only`` (the default) it must have an adapter that returns a :class:`PhysicsDataBundle` — a reader
   that stops at "raw trajectories" is not readable *into this library's contract*, and the catalogue's
   ``readable`` flag alone does not say that;
3. an archive whose licence text marks it non-commercial is dropped when ``commercial_ok`` is false — the text is
   quoted in the refusal rather than interpreted;
4. the rest are ordered by priority (P0 first), then by whether the licence was verified here, then by id. No score,
   no weights: the tie-break is name-stable so two runs choose the same archive.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.read import choose
    >>> choose("data")["id"]             # P0, licence verified, first by name among equals
    'cfdbench'
    >>> choose("inverse")["id"]          # the subsurface archive is the only one that feeds identification
    'spe10'
    >>> choose("data", prefer="pdebench")["id"]
    'pdebench'

classes.doc: How one catalogued archive becomes a bundle: the callable and the arguments it insists on.

Whether a licence text forbids commercial use — matched as substrings, so the caller can quote what matched.

archive by id does not go through :func:`choose`, and a gate written twice is a gate that disagrees with itself.

``prefer`` names an archive to use if it survived the filters — the escape hatch for a caller that knows which

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.remote_hdf5
children.doc:
Read an HDF5 file over HTTP without downloading it, or from disk, behind one small interface.

The datasets this matters for are 1-13 GB each (PDEBench) or 2-20 TB each (The Well): a 5 GB download to read one
sample is not a workflow, and a benchmark that needs it never runs in CI. HDF5 is built for this -- it keeps its
metadata (superblock, B-tree, chunk index) in a few kilobytes and reads only the chunks a slice touches -- so the
only thing missing is a file object that can seek over HTTP. That is :class:`HTTPRangeFile`: a seekable
``io.RawIOBase`` that answers each ``read`` with one HTTP ``Range`` request.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.remote_hdf5 import open_hdf5
    >>> with open_hdf5("https://.../Sod6.hdf5") as f:      # or a local path
    ...     print(f["density"].shape)

Two behaviours worth knowing:

* a file at or below ``max_cache_bytes`` (64 MiB by default) is fetched once, streamed into memory, and served
  from there -- for a 5 MB case that is one request instead of a few hundred;
* a bigger file is read by range only. Metadata reads are cheap; reading a *slice* is cheap; iterating every
  element of a chunked dataset over HTTP is not, and the docstrings of the adapters say so.

The generic-URL handling (resolve the redirect of a DOI landing endpoint, then range-read the S3 target) is what
makes DaRUS -- where PDEBench lives -- work; Hugging Face's ``resolve`` endpoints behave the same way.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.spe10
children.doc:
SPE10: the Tenth SPE Comparative Solution Project model 2, read as the bundle a Darcy problem needs.

SPE10 model 2 (Christie & Blunt, 2001) is the heterogeneous-permeability case that reservoir and Darcy-flow work
reports on: a 60 x 220 x 85 corner-point-free Cartesian grid of 1 122 000 cells, 20 x 10 x 2 ft each, whose top 35
layers are the Tarbert formation and whose bottom 50 are the fluvial Upper Ness. The SPE distributes it as one archive
(``por_perm_case2a.zip``) holding two ASCII tables, and this module turns them into a bundle.

The layout below was read off the archive itself (downloaded from the SPE page while writing this module), not from a
description of it:

``spe_perm.dat``
    6 values per line, 561 000 lines: ``kx ky kz`` for two cells. The value for cell ``(i, j, k)`` is at
    ``index = i + 60 * (j + 220 * k)`` -- **i varies fastest**. That ordering is not stated in the file; it was checked
    against the model's own structure: read that way the per-layer mean permeability jumps by a factor of two at layer
    36, which is where the Tarbert formation ends, and read the other way (k fastest) the layers are statistically
    indistinguishable.
``spe_phi.dat``
    6 values per line, 187 000 lines: one porosity per cell, same ordering.

Two limits that are recorded in every bundle rather than smoothed over:

* **which of the three permeability values is kx, ky or kz is a convention, not a property of the file.** The three
  columns have the same median (about 3 mD), the same mean (255 mD) and the same spread, so the numbers cannot say
  which is which; the bundle names them ``kx``/``ky``/``kz`` in the order the SPE documentation is always quoted in and
  says so in its metadata.
* **the archive states no licence.** SPE's dataset page describes the model and links the archive without terms, so
  ``license`` is a required argument here: this module will not write "unknown" into a file somebody redistributes.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets import spe10
    >>> bundle = spe10.load_bundle("spe10/spe_perm.dat", "spe10/spe_phi.dat", license="SPE CSP dataset terms")  # doctest: +SKIP

functions.name: read_perm
functions.sig: (path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, shape: Sequence[int] = SHAPE) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Permeability as ``(nx, ny, nz, 3)`` in mD, the three components in the order the file lists them.

``shape`` is the grid to reshape onto: the fine grid by default, and a coarser one when the caller is reading an
upscaled copy laid out the same way.

functions.name: read_phi
functions.sig: (path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, shape: Sequence[int] = SHAPE) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Porosity as ``(nx, ny, nz)``, dimensionless, in the same cell order as the permeability.

functions.name: load_bundle
functions.sig: (perm: str | os.PathLike[str] | np.ndarray, phi: str | os.PathLike[str] | np.ndarray | None = None, *, license: str, source: str = '', units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, components: tuple[str, str, str] = ('kx', 'ky', 'kz'), shape: Sequence[int] = SHAPE) -> Any
functions.doc:
The model as a bundle: three permeability components and the porosity, on the grid SPE describes.

``perm``/``phi`` are paths to the archive's tables or arrays already read. The axes are cell **centres** in feet
from the top of the model (``z`` grows downwards, as a reservoir depth does) and the fields are declared
``cell``-centred, which is what they are.

children.name: pinneapple_data.datasets.the_well
children.doc:
The Well: read its HDF5 trajectories into the universal schema.

The Well (Ohana et al., NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks, "The Well: a Large-Scale Collection of Diverse
Physics Simulations for Machine Learning"; code BSD-3-Clause, data hosted per scenario at
`huggingface.co/polymathic-ai <https://huggingface.co/polymathic-ai>`_) holds ~15 TB of physics simulations in 16+
scenarios, every file 2-22 GB. Like PDEBench, it is read here through range requests
(:mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.remote_hdf5`), so one trajectory costs megabytes instead of a terabyte-scale
download.

The layout, taken from the layout its own loader reads (``the_well/data/datasets.py`` v1.2.0)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
``/dimensions``
    one dataset per axis (``time``, ``x``, ``y``, ``z``), ``attrs["spatial_dims"]`` naming the spatial ones; each
    axis carries ``attrs["sample_varying"]`` (and the time axis ``attrs["time_varying"]``).
``/t0_fields``, ``/t1_fields``, ``/t2_fields``
    the fields, grouped by tensor rank, ``attrs["field_names"]``; every dataset is ``(n_trajectories, n_time,
    *spatial)``, with the time axis absent when ``attrs["time_varying"]`` is false.
``/boundary_conditions``
    one dataset per axis with ``attrs["bc_type"]`` and shape ``(n_trajectories, 2)`` (low, high).
``/scalars``
    ``attrs["field_names"]``; each is per-sample, per-time or constant.
Root attributes: ``dataset_name``, ``grid_type``, ``n_spatial_dims``, ``n_trajectories``.

This reader is exercised in the tests on a file written to that layout (a reproduction of it, not a downloaded
multi-gigabyte scenario -- the download is what the reader exists to avoid). It reads: the fields with their
canonical axes, the boundary conditions as schema ``BoundaryCondition`` entries, the scalars as ``Parameter``
and ``metadata``, and the per-sample axes that vary.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.the_well import open_the_well
    >>> with open_the_well("https://huggingface.co/datasets/polymathic-ai/rayleigh_benard/"
    ...                    "resolve/main/data/train/rayleigh_benard_Rayleigh_1e10_Prandtl_1.hdf5") as f:
    ...     f.dataset_name, f.spatial_dims, f.fields

    from pinneapple_data.datasets import load_dataset, list_datasets

    data = load_dataset("burgers_1d")     # physics

children.name: pinneapple_data.doe
pinneapple_data.doe.campaign
children.doc:
Plan a simulation campaign: which cases to run, in which order, and what they add to what already ran.

from pinneapple_data.doe import plan_campaign
plan = plan_campaign(space, n=40, method="maximin", existing=done_runs, existing_id_column="run_id")
plan.cases                 # case_id, priority, every parameter, nearest existing run and distance
plan.summary()             # coverage before / after, redundant cases removed, compute saved
plan.study_result()        # pinneapple_data.contracts.StudyResult (study_type "doe")
plan.dataset_skeleton(outputs=["Cl", "Cd"])   # DatasetSpec with status "skeleton" for the surrogate step

methods.name: view
methods.doc:
The plan in unit-cube coordinates for a scatter view: the free parameter ``names``, ``planned`` cases,
``existing`` runs (when given) and ``dropped`` repeats (when any), rounded to ``digits``; with the axis
``labels`` (name and unit), ``kinds``, the ``values`` of categorical parameters and the ``bounds``
(``[low, high, log]``) of the numeric ones.

methods.name: checks
methods.doc: Checks that ran on this plan, each with its value.

methods.name: dataset_skeleton
methods.sig: (outputs: Sequence[str] = (), units: dict[str, str] | None = None, app: str = 'campaign') -> DatasetSpec
methods.doc: The dataset these runs will make: inputs and declared outputs, no results yet (status "skeleton").

functions.name: plan_campaign
functions.sig: (space: ParameterSpace, n: int | None = None, method: str = 'lhs', *, existing = None, existing_id_column: str | None = None, outputs: Sequence[str] = (), seed: int = 0, levels: int | dict[str, int] = 3, tol: float | None = None, drop_repeats: bool = True, feasible: Callable[[Any], np.ndarray] | None = None, name: str | None = None, id_prefix: str = 'case') -> CampaignPlan
functions.doc:
Design ``n`` cases (default ``space.budget``), drop those repeating an existing run (``drop_repeats``), order
the rest by priority and measure the coverage of the plan, of what exists, and of both together. Existing cases
outside the space (bounds or constraints) are left out of the coverage and listed in
``redundancy["existing_outside_space"]``.

children.summary: Plan a simulation campaign: which cases to run, in which order, and what they add to what already ran.

children.name: pinneapple_data.doe.coverage
children.doc:
How well a set of cases covers a parameter space, which planned cases repeat what already ran, and in which
order to run them.

All distances are in the unit hypercube of the free parameters (``ParameterSpace.to_unit``), so a parameter in
metres and one in pascals weigh the same; categories and integers sit at the centres of their cells.

functions.name: coverage
functions.sig: (unit: np.ndarray, names: list[str] | None = None, *, n_probe: int = 2 ** 14, seed: int = 0, bins_2d: int | None = None, levels: dict[str, int] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Space-coverage metrics of points in [0, 1]^d.

``discrepancy``      centred L2 discrepancy (scipy ``qmc.discrepancy``, method "CD"): lower is more uniform
``min_distance``     smallest distance between two points (0: duplicates)
``mean_nn_distance`` mean distance to the nearest other point
``fill_distance``    largest distance from any probe point of the cube to its nearest case: the biggest hole
``ideal_spacing``    (1/n)^(1/d), the spacing of a regular grid with n points, to read the distances against
``projection_1d``    per parameter: fraction of n equal bins holding at least one case; for a discrete parameter
                     with k values (``levels``), of min(n, k) bins
``projection_2d``    per pair of parameters: fraction of b x b cells holding a case (b = floor(sqrt(n)))

functions.name: redundancy
functions.sig: (planned_unit: np.ndarray, existing_unit: np.ndarray | None = None, *, tol: float | None = None, existing_ids: list[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Which planned cases (nearly) repeat an existing case or another planned case.

``tol`` is a distance in the unit cube (default 1 % of its diagonal, 0.01 * sqrt(d)). Returns per planned case
the nearest existing case and distance, and the flags; plus the near-duplicate pairs inside the existing data
(compute that was already spent twice).

functions.name: prioritize
functions.sig: (planned_unit: np.ndarray, existing_unit: np.ndarray | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run order: greedy maximin over the planned cases, starting from what already exists, so every prefix of the
list covers the space as evenly as possible (stop the campaign early and the cases run are still spread out).
``score`` is each case's distance to everything before it (existing included): the information it adds.

children.summary: How well a set of cases covers a parameter space, which planned cases repeat what already ran, and in which order to run them.

children.name: pinneapple_data.doe.designs
children.doc:
Designs of experiments over a :class:`~pinneapple_data.contracts.ParameterSpace`.

Every design is built in the unit hypercube of the free parameters and mapped to values by the space (log scales,
integers, categories), then filtered by the space's bounds and constraints (and an optional ``feasible`` callable
for checks that are not expressions, such as a geometry validity test).

=======================  =====================================================================================
``lhs``                  Latin hypercube (scipy.stats.qmc), one point per stratum in every 1-D projection
``maximin``              the Latin hypercube with the largest minimum distance among ``n_restarts`` random ones
``sobol`` / ``halton``   scrambled low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol balance needs n = 2^m)
``random``               uniform random (reference only: clusters and gaps)
``full_factorial``       every combination of ``levels`` per parameter (all values of categories / integers)
``fractional_factorial`` two-level 2^(k-p) design with generated factors; reports the generators and resolution
``infill``               sequential: new points as far as possible from the existing cases (greedy maximin over a
                         Sobol candidate pool); with ``outputs`` the distance is weighted up where the existing
                         outputs vary most among neighbours (adaptive refinement)
=======================  =====================================================================================

When constraints remove points, more candidates are drawn and the design keeps the feasible ones: for ``lhs``,
``sobol``, ``halton`` and ``random`` the first ``n`` in sequence order, for ``maximin`` and ``infill`` a greedy
maximin subset. The Latin-hypercube stratification is then only approximate; the coverage metrics show by how much.

classes.name: Design
classes.doc: The cases of a design: values (DataFrame with every parameter), unit coordinates and how they were made.

functions.name: design
functions.sig: (space: ParameterSpace, n: int, method: str = 'lhs', *, seed: int = 0, existing = None, outputs: Sequence[str] = (), levels: int | dict[str, int] = 3, n_restarts: int = 20, feasible: Callable[[Any], np.ndarray] | None = None, max_candidates: int = 200000) -> Design
functions.doc:
``n`` cases of ``space`` by ``method`` (see the module docstring). ``existing`` is a DataFrame of cases
already run (a column per parameter, plus ``outputs`` for adaptive infill).

functions.name: design_size
functions.sig: (space: ParameterSpace, method: str = 'lhs', n: int | None = None, levels: int | dict[str, int] = 3, *, feasible: Callable[[Any], np.ndarray] | None = None) -> int
functions.doc:
How many cases :func:`design` (and so :func:`~pinneapple_data.doe.plan_campaign`, before it drops repeats of
existing runs) returns for these arguments, without drawing a sampled design.

``n`` defaults to ``space.budget`` as in ``plan_campaign``. Sampled methods (``lhs``, ``maximin``, ``sobol``,
``halton``, ``random``, ``infill``) return exactly ``n``. The factorial ones are built (they are cheap and
deterministic) and the constraints of ``space`` and ``feasible`` applied, so the count is the planned one: a
``fractional_factorial`` has the 2^(k-p) runs :func:`fractional_factorial_unit` chooses, a ``full_factorial``
the product of its levels (integer parameters with fewer values than ``levels`` use each value once).
A factorial with no feasible point gives 0 (``design`` raises).

functions.name: fractional_factorial_unit
functions.doc:
Two-level 2^(k-p) design with at least ``n`` runs (or 2^k if smaller): the first k-p factors are crossed in
full, each further factor is the product of a distinct subset of them (largest subsets first, which keeps the
resolution high). Returns unit coordinates (0 / 1) and the generators and resolution.

functions.name: greedy_maximin
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, n: int, fixed: np.ndarray | None = None, weights_fixed: np.ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Indices of ``n`` of ``points`` picked one by one, each the farthest from those already picked and from
``fixed``. ``weights_fixed`` (one per fixed point, >= 1) favours the neighbourhoods to refine: a candidate's
distance to the fixed points is multiplied by the weight of its nearest fixed point.

children.summary: Designs of experiments over a ~pinneapple_data.contracts.ParameterSpace.

children.doc:
Design of experiments for simulation campaigns: designs, coverage, redundancy, priorities, campaign plans.

Built on :mod:`pinneapple_data.contracts` (a ``ParameterSpace`` in, a ``StudyResult`` and a ``DatasetSpec``
skeleton out) and ``scipy.stats.qmc``. The case files per solver (OpenFOAM, CalculiX, Python) are written by
:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.campaign_cases`.
children.summary: Design of experiments for simulation campaigns: designs, coverage, redundancy, priorities, campaign plans.

children.name: pinneapple_data.expressions
children.doc:
Safe evaluation of constraint expressions such as ``"chord - 2 * thickness >= 0.01"``.

Only arithmetic, comparisons, ``and`` / ``or`` / ``not``, parameter names, numbers, strings and a few math functions
are allowed; anything else (attribute access, calls to other functions, subscripts, lambdas) is refused before the
expression runs. Every name is a column, so one call checks a whole table of cases at once.

The expression is interpreted node by node, never handed to ``eval``: this is the evaluator for any formula a user
sends to a server (constraints, boundary values, source terms). ``functions=`` replaces the callable table and
:func:`check` validates an expression for another consumer (e.g. before ``sympy.sympify``).

classes.name: ExpressionError
classes.doc: The expression uses something that is not allowed, or a name that is not a parameter.

functions.name: names_in
functions.doc: Parameter names an expression refers to (function names excluded).

functions.name: evaluate
functions.sig: (expression: str, values: Mapping[str, Any], functions: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Evaluate ``expression`` with ``values`` (name -> scalar or column) and return a boolean (or numeric) array.
``functions``: the names it may call (default :data:`FUNCTIONS`).

functions.name: check
functions.sig: (expression: str, names: Iterable[str], functions: Iterable[str] = (), strings: bool = False) -> None
functions.doc:
Raise :class:`ExpressionError` unless ``expression`` uses only the grammar above, the variables ``names`` and
calls of ``functions`` (and no string literals unless ``strings``).

children.summary: Safe evaluation of constraint expressions such as "chord - 2 * thickness >= 0.01".

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill
pinneapple_data.formfill.extract
children.doc:
Read datasheets and specifications, find each answer a form asks for, and keep where every value came from.

Pipeline: ``read_document`` (text per page plus the tables pdfplumber finds) -> ``extract_rules`` (the spec's label
patterns, applied to table cells and to text lines) -> optional ``llm.extract_with_llm`` (a local Ollama model) ->
``compile`` (one decision per item: value from the highest-priority document, conflicts and gaps reported).

Every candidate keeps the document, page and the exact text it was read from, so an engineer can check any value
in one click instead of trusting the tool.

methods.name: record
methods.doc: The compiled data for other forms and calculations: item -> value, unit, SI value and source.

functions.name: read_document
functions.sig: (source: Union[str, bytes], name: str = '', role: str = '', ocr: str = 'auto', max_ocr_pages: int = 30) -> Document
functions.doc:
A PDF (path or bytes) or plain text (``.txt``/``.md`` path, or bytes that are not a PDF).

``ocr``: "auto" reads the pages without a text layer (scans) with Tesseract when it is installed; "always" reads
every page with OCR; "never" leaves scanned pages unread (listed in ``unread_pages``).

functions.name: parse_value
functions.doc: Interpret ``text`` as an answer to ``f``; ``None`` when it does not look like one.

functions.name: extract_rules
functions.doc:
Candidates for every item of ``spec`` whose label appears in ``doc`` (tables first, then text lines), plus
the rows of the spec's tables.

functions.name: check_answer
functions.doc: An engineer's answer for ``f``, validated (``ValueError`` names the accepted options).

functions.name: compile
functions.sig: (docs: Sequence[Document], candidates: Iterable[Candidate], spec: FormSpec, overrides: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None) -> Compilation
functions.doc:
One decision per item of ``spec``. Documents earlier in ``docs`` win conflicts (order = priority); the conflict is still
reported with every source. ``overrides`` (an engineer's answers) win over everything and are marked as such.

children.summary: Read datasheets and specifications, find each answer a form asks for, and keep where every value came from.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.fill
children.doc:
Write a compilation into the user's copy of a fillable PDF form.

Text fields get the value as written in the source (number and unit, e.g. ``15 barg``); check boxes and radio
groups get the export state from the spec. Items in ``spec.left_blank`` (date, signature...) are never filled: a
form that certifies requirements must be reviewed and signed by a person.

functions.name: pdf_widgets
functions.doc:
Every form widget of a PDF: qualified name, type (``/Tx``, ``/Btn``...), page, tooltip, button states and
whether it belongs to a radio group.

functions.name: form_values
functions.sig: (comp: Compilation, spec: Optional[FormSpec] = None) -> Tuple[Dict[str, str], Dict[str, str]]
functions.doc: ``(text fields, button states)`` for the PDF, from the decisions and the table rows.

functions.name: fill_pdf
functions.sig: (blank_pdf: bytes, comp: Compilation, spec: Optional[FormSpec] = None, extra_text: Optional[Mapping[str, str]] = None) -> bytes
functions.doc: The filled form as PDF bytes. ``blank_pdf`` is the user's copy of the fillable form ``spec`` describes.

functions.name: read_filled

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.llm
children.doc:
Optional extraction with a local LLM served by Ollama, for documents the label rules cannot read (free-form
specifications, odd layouts, forms whose items have no usual label).

Documents never leave the machine: the text of each document (with its tables and page numbers) is sent to an
Ollama server you run (``ollama serve``), by default ``http://localhost:11434``. The model answers in a JSON schema
built from the form spec (Ollama structured outputs) with, for each item it finds, the value, the page and the
**exact text it read it from**. An answer is kept only if

* that quote is found in the document's own text (whitespace and case ignored), and
* for text, numbers and quantities, the value itself is in the quote,

so a value the model made up is rejected and listed, never silently used. Accepted values go through the same parser
as the rule-based ones (units, yes/no, options).

Configuration: ``OllamaClient(url, model)`` or the environment variables ``OLLAMA_HOST`` (server URL) and
``PINNEAPPLE_OLLAMA_MODEL`` (any model you pulled with ``ollama pull`` that supports structured outputs). Only the
Python standard library is used.

classes.name: OllamaClient
classes.sig: (url: Optional[str] = None, model: Optional[str] = None, timeout: float = 600.0, num_ctx: int = 16384)
classes.doc: Minimal client for the Ollama HTTP API (``/api/chat``, ``/api/tags``).

methods.name: available
methods.doc: The server answers and the configured model is pulled.

methods.name: chat_json

functions.doc: Page-marked text of a document, its tables written as ``cell | cell`` rows.

functions.name: verify_quote

functions.doc: Page (1-based) where ``quote`` occurs in the document text, preferring the stated page; ``None`` if absent.

functions.name: extract_with_llm

functions.doc: ``(accepted candidates, rejected answers with the reason)`` for one document.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.ocr
children.doc:
OCR for scanned pages (pages without a text layer), with Tesseract.

Datasheets are tables, and table grid lines are what OCR gets wrong: a border next to "1.27" is read as "427". So each
page is rendered at 300 dpi, deskewed, its grid lines are detected and erased before Tesseract reads it, and the
detected lines are then used to put every word back in its table cell. The result has the same shape as a page with a
text layer (text lines + table rows), so the same rules read it, and every word keeps Tesseract's confidence: values
read by OCR are marked as such, with their confidence, for the engineer to check against the scan.

Needs the ``tesseract`` program (``apt install tesseract-ocr``, or set ``TESSERACT_CMD``); page rendering uses
pypdfium2, which pdfplumber already depends on.

functions.doc: OCR one page image (PIL).

functions.sig: (pdf_bytes: bytes, index: int, dpi: int = DPI) -> OcrPage
functions.doc: OCR page ``index`` (0-based) of a PDF.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.pipeline

One call from source documents to a compiled form, and the helpers a front end needs around it.

from pinneapple_data.formfill import compile_documents, get_spec
comp, rejected = compile_documents([("rfq.pdf", data, "customer")], get_spec("api610_pump"))

functions.name: compile_documents
functions.sig: (docs: Sequence[Tuple[str, bytes, str]], spec: FormSpec, client: Any = None, overrides: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None, max_ocr_pages: Optional[int] = None) -> Tuple[Compilation, List[Dict[str, Any]]]
functions.doc:
Read every ``(name, data, role)`` document, extract candidates with the rules of ``spec`` (and with the local
LLM ``client`` too, when given) and compile them into one decision per form item.

A failing LLM extraction never fails the call: the rule-based candidates stand and the failure is reported.
Returns ``(compilation, rejected)``; ``rejected`` lists the LLM candidates that were dropped, each with its
``reason`` and ``doc``.

an unknown key or an invalid value raises ``ValueError`` with a message for the user.

File name for the filled form: ``<spec id>_<value of spec.filename_key or "filled">_<YYYYMMDD>.pdf``, made of
safe characters only.

The compiled datasheet as a PDF (needs reportlab): every item of the spec with its value and source, the open
items (missing required data, conflicts between documents) first, side-by-side columns where the spec has them
(shell side | tube side), the table rows and the documents read.

This is the tool's own layout, marked as a draft for engineering review. It is the output for templates that have no
fillable official form, and a data compilation report for those that do.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.spec
children.doc:
What a form asks for, how documents phrase each item, and where each answer goes in the fillable PDF.

A ``FormSpec`` is data, not code: the same engine reads documents, compiles answers and fills the PDF for any spec.
Specs come from three places:

* built-in templates (``pinneapple_data.formfill.specs``, e.g. ASME Form U-DR-1),
* a JSON file (``FormSpec.load``): copy a template or a generated spec, add label patterns, mark required items,
* any fillable PDF (``FormSpec.from_pdf``): one item per AcroForm field, labelled from its tooltip or name. Rules find
  the items whose label is written in the documents; the local LLM finds the rest.

Field kinds: ``text``, ``quantity`` (number + unit, compared in SI), ``number``, ``bool`` (yes/no), ``choice`` (one of
``options``), ``multi`` (several of ``options``).

classes.name: TableSpec
classes.doc:
A repeated-row item (nozzle schedule, line list...): found as a document table whose header matches ``header``
(every regex must match some header cell), filled into ``pdf_rows`` (one dict column -> PDF field per row).

methods.name: describe
methods.doc:
What a front end needs to show the form: identity, sections, and per field its label, kind, options,
whether it is required and whether the extraction rules can read it from a document; per table its
columns and number of rows.

methods.name: from_pdf
methods.doc:
One item per AcroForm field of ``blank_pdf``. Text fields become ``text`` items, a check box ``bool``, a radio
group ``choice`` (its export states as options). The label is the field's tooltip (``/TU``) or its name made
readable; items with a readable label also get a label pattern, so the rules can find them.

children.summary: What a form asks for, how documents phrase each item, and where each answer goes in the fillable PDF.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.specs
pinneapple_data.formfill.specs.asme_udr1
children.doc:
Built-in template: ASME BPVC Section VIII Division 1 Form U-DR-1, and where each answer goes in its fillable PDF.

Each ``Field`` is one answer on the form (User's Design Requirements for Single-Chamber Pressure Vessels, ASME BPVC
Section VIII, Division 1, Nonmandatory Appendix KK). ``pdf`` names the AcroForm field it is written to; for check
boxes and radio groups ``states`` maps an answer to the ``(field, export state)`` pair that represents it. The PDF
field names come from the 07/25 revision of the form; many are generic (``Group10``, ``Text7``), so the mapping was
made by overlaying each widget's rectangle on the rendered page (see ``tests/test_formfill.py``).

``patterns`` are the phrasings used in process datasheets, mechanical datasheets and client specifications for the
same item (case-insensitive regular expressions, matched at a label position). ``quantity`` names the physical
quantity for unit-aware comparison between documents. ``required`` marks the items without which a manufacturer
cannot start the design; missing ones are reported as data gaps.

The blank form itself is ASME's copyrighted document and is not shipped here: users upload their copy.
children.summary: Built-in template: ASME BPVC Section VIII Division 1 Form U-DR-1, and where each answer goes in its fillable PDF.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.specs.psv
children.doc:
Built-in template: pressure relief valve datasheet, with the data API 520 Part I (sizing) and API 526 (flanged steel
valves) ask for. The output is a compiled datasheet generated by the tool, not a reproduction of a standard's form.

Data usually comes from the process datasheet or the relief load summary (relieving case, rate, fluid properties),
the PSV sizing calculation (orifice) and the piping/valve specifications (connections, materials).
children.summary: Built-in template: pressure relief valve datasheet, with the data API 520 Part I (sizing) and API 526 (flanged steel valves) ask for.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.specs.pump
children.doc:
Built-in template: centrifugal pump datasheet, with the data API 610 asks the purchaser for. The output is a
compiled datasheet generated by the tool, not a reproduction of the standard's data sheet.

Liquid and operating data usually comes from the process datasheet and the hydraulic calculation (NPSH available);
construction choices from the client's pump specification; site and driver data from the electrical and site
specifications.
children.summary: Built-in template: centrifugal pump datasheet, with the data API 610 asks the purchaser for.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.specs.shell_tube
children.doc:
Built-in template: shell-and-tube heat exchanger datasheet, with the data a TEMA specification sheet and API 660 ask
for. The output is a compiled datasheet generated by the tool, not a reproduction of a standard's form.

Process data (fluids, flows, temperatures, pressures, fouling) usually comes from the process datasheet, one column per
side; construction data from the mechanical datasheet and the client's specifications. Tables with a "shell side" and
a "tube side" column are read cell by cell.
children.summary: Built-in template: shell-and-tube heat exchanger datasheet, with the data a TEMA specification sheet and API 660 ask for.

children.name: pinneapple_data.formfill.specs.tank
children.doc:
Built-in template: atmospheric storage tank datasheet, with the data API 650 asks the purchaser for (Annex L lists
them). The output is a compiled datasheet generated by the tool, not a reproduction of the standard's data sheet.

Process data (product, specific gravity, temperatures, fill and empty rates) usually comes from the process datasheet;
design data from the mechanical datasheet, the client's tank specification and the site data (wind, seismic, snow).
children.summary: Built-in template: atmospheric storage tank datasheet, with the data API 650 asks the purchaser for (Annex L lists them).

children.doc:
Built-in form templates. Add one by writing a module that builds a ``FormSpec`` and registering it here, or ship it
as JSON and load it with ``FormSpec.load``.
children.summary: Built-in form templates.

children.doc:
Fill engineering forms from the documents that hold the data: read datasheets and specifications, find every item a
form asks for with its source, report conflicts between documents and missing data, and fill the fillable PDF.

The engine is generic; a ``FormSpec`` says what one form asks for. Built-in: ASME Form U-DR-1. Any other fillable
PDF works through ``FormSpec.from_pdf`` (or a JSON spec), and a local Ollama model can read what the rules miss.

>>> from pinneapple_data import formfill as ff
>>> spec = ff.get_spec("asme_u-dr-1")                       # or ff.FormSpec.from_pdf(blank) / ff.FormSpec.load(path)
>>> docs = [ff.read_document(p) for p in ("spec.pdf", "process.pdf", "mech.pdf")]      # priority order
>>> comp = ff.compile(docs, [c for d in docs for c in ff.extract_rules(d, spec)], spec)
>>> comp.gaps(), comp.conflicts(), comp.record()            # record(): the data for other forms and calculations
>>> pdf = ff.fill_pdf(open("blank.pdf", "rb").read(), comp)
children.summary: Fill engineering forms from the documents that hold the data: read datasheets and specifications, find every item a form asks for with its source, report conflicts between documents and missing data, ...

children.name: pinneapple_data.geometry_features
children.doc:
Geometry featurization: surface point-cloud sampling and a coarse
signed-distance-field (SDF) grid from a triangle mesh — generic inputs
(vertices/faces arrays, matching this package's own `stl_import.STLMesh`
convention), no file-format or storage coupling. Useful as a preprocessing
step for any geometry-conditioned model (e.g. a GNN or point-cloud PINN that
needs an explicit distance-to-surface feature).

Requires `trimesh` (only used internally for surface sampling and the
signed-distance query — both nontrivial geometry algorithms not worth
re-implementing).

functions.name: sample_point_cloud
functions.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, faces: np.ndarray, n_samples: int = 2048) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Sample `n_samples` points uniformly (area-weighted) from a mesh's
surface. `n_samples` is silently capped at 3x the face count for a very
coarse mesh, since sampling far more points than the mesh has resolution
to support doesn't add real information.

functions.name: compute_sdf_grid
functions.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, faces: np.ndarray, grid_resolution: int = 16, bounds: Optional[np.ndarray] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Evaluate a signed distance field on a regular grid spanning the mesh's
bounding box (or a caller-supplied `bounds` = [[xmin,ymin,zmin],
[xmax,ymax,zmax]], e.g. to featurize several meshes on one shared grid).

Returns {"points": (grid_resolution^3, 3), "sdf": (grid_resolution^3,),
"grid_shape": [grid_resolution]*3}. Positive values are outside the mesh,
negative inside (trimesh's convention).

functions.name: featurize_mesh
functions.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, faces: np.ndarray, n_point_cloud_samples: int = 2048, sdf_grid_resolution: int = 16) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Convenience wrapper: point cloud + SDF grid in one call, with
per-stage errors reported rather than raised (a degenerate/non-watertight
mesh may still yield a usable point cloud even if the SDF query fails).

children.name: pinneapple_data.graph
children.doc:
Geometry as a graph: what a mesh-graph network (MeshGraphNet and family) needs, from a bundle.

A grid or a mesh becomes nodes with features and edges with geometry:

* **nodes**: position, and the field values the caller names (or the nodal fields of the bundle), flattened to
  ``(n_nodes, n_features)``;
* **edges**: for a structured grid, the nearest neighbours along each spatial axis at ``t = 0`` (or a chosen step) --
  the stencil a finite-volume mesh has, without inventing long-range links; for an unstructured mesh, the unique
  edges of the element connectivity, which *is* the mesh's own adjacency;
* **edge features**: the displacement vector and its length, which is what a mesh-graph network conditions on.

Everything is returned as numpy arrays in a small :class:`Graph` dataclass: ``torch_geometric`` is optional and is
only touched by :func:`to_torch_geometric`, so a project that already has PyG gets a ``Data`` object and one that does
not still gets the graph.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.graph import grid_graph
    >>> g = grid_graph(bundle, fields=("u",), step=0)
    >>> g.pos.shape, g.edge_index.shape, g.edge_attr.shape
    ((1024, 1), (2, 2046), (2046, 2))

classes.name: Graph
classes.doc: Nodes with features, and directed edges with their geometry (both directions, as message passing expects).

functions.name: grid_graph
functions.sig: (bundle: Any, *, fields: Sequence[str] = (), step: int = 0, stencil: int = 1) -> Graph
functions.doc: The graph of a structured bundle at one time step: neighbours along each spatial axis.

functions.name: mesh_graph
functions.doc: The graph of an unstructured bundle: the element connectivity's own edges, once each.

functions.name: to_torch_geometric
functions.doc: A ``torch_geometric.data.Data`` of the same graph (needs PyG; nothing else in this module imports it).

children.summary: Geometry as a graph: what a mesh-graph network (MeshGraphNet and family) needs, from a bundle.

children.name: pinneapple_data.grf_sampler
children.doc:
Gaussian Random Field (GRF) input-function sampler, the standard way to
draw random forcing/coefficient functions u(x) for operator-learning
benchmarks (e.g. Lu, Jin & Karniadakis 2019, "DeepONet", arXiv:1910.03193,
which draws every one of its input functions from a zero-mean GRF with an
RBF/squared-exponential covariance kernel, length scale 0.2 by default).
Useful any time a dataset needs many independent random functions sharing a
common smoothness/correlation structure — not just for DeepONet.

Design (1D, `sample_grf_batch`): one Cholesky factorization of the RBF
covariance on a fixed fine grid (n_grid points) per BATCH of draws, not one
per draw — draws are just L @ standard_normal, and each draw is wrapped in a
CubicSpline so downstream ODE/PDE solvers can query u(x) at whatever points
their own integrator lands on, not just the n_grid grid nodes (this is the
literature-standard implementation approach — DeepXDE's own GRF class does
the same thing: a spline over a fine grid, not GP-reconditioning at
arbitrary query time, which would be O(m^3) per query batch instead of
O(n_grid) once per draw).

Design (2D, `sample_grf_2d_batch`): a direct 2D generalization of the 1D
approach (Cholesky of the full covariance matrix) would need an (nx*ny) x
(nx*ny) covariance matrix — O((nx*ny)^3) Cholesky, e.g. a modest 64x64 grid
is already a 4096x4096 factorization per draw. Instead this uses the
standard spectral-synthesis / circulant-embedding-adjacent FFT method for
stationary GRFs (Wiener-Khinchin theorem: the power spectral density of a
stationary random field is the Fourier transform of its covariance
function): draw white noise on an (nx, ny) grid, multiply its 2D FFT by the
square root of the target covariance kernel's power spectral density,
inverse-FFT, take the real part. This is O(nx*ny*log(nx*ny)) per draw and is
a named, textbook method (see e.g. Lang & Potthoff 2011, "Fast simulation of
Gaussian random fields"), not hand-rolled.

The covariance kernel matched is the same RBF/squared-exponential family
used by the 1D sampler: C(r) = exp(-r^2 / (2*l^2)). Its 2D continuous
Fourier transform is itself Gaussian in wavenumber space, so sqrt(PSD(k)) ~
exp(-l^2*|k|^2/4) up to an overall multiplicative constant — that constant
is irrelevant here because every draw is renormalized to zero mean / unit
variance post-synthesis (the discrete FFT's own normalization convention
and grid resolution both affect the raw variance, so matching a target
variance by construction is fragile; renormalizing empirically is the
standard, robust fix, since only the spatial correlation structure matters
for most downstream uses, not an absolute scale — callers apply their own
amplitude/sigma multiplier on top).

classes.doc: One sampled function u(x), x in [x_min, x_max].

methods.name: sensors
methods.doc:
u evaluated at a fixed set of sensor points (an operator-learning
branch net's input — m points, conventionally evenly spaced).

classes.doc: One sampled 2D field u(x,y), (x,y) in [0,1]x[0,1] (normalized).

u evaluated on a fixed m_x-by-m_y sensor grid (an operator-learning

functions.doc:
Draw n_draws independent zero-mean GRF paths sharing ONE Cholesky
factorization of the RBF covariance on a common fine grid.

functions.name: sample_grf_paths
functions.sig: (n_draws: int, x_min: float = 0.0, x_max: float = 1.0, n_grid: int = 1000, length_scale: float = 0.2, jitter: float = 1e-10, seed: Optional[int] = None) -> List[GRFDraw]
functions.doc:
Alias for sample_grf_batch (kept for readability at call sites that
draw a single small batch rather than a full dataset-generation pass).

functions.name: sample_grf_2d_batch
functions.sig: (n_draws: int, nx: int = 64, ny: int = 64, length_scale: float = 0.2, seed: Optional[int] = None) -> List[GRFDraw2D]
functions.doc:
Draw n_draws independent zero-mean, unit-variance 2D GRF paths on the
normalized [0,1]x[0,1] domain via FFT spectral synthesis (see module
docstring above). One (nx,ny) white-noise draw + one 2D FFT + one
inverse 2D FFT per sample — no shared factorization to amortize across
draws the way sample_grf_batch's Cholesky is (the FFT method has no
equivalent expensive-precompute step to share), so batching here is just
a loop, not a performance-motivated primitive like the 1D version.
