children.name: pinneapple_data.lineage.graph
children.doc:
Engineering model lineage: artifacts (CAD, mesh, simulation, dataset, model, prediction, ...) linked by "derived
from" edges into a digital thread, with the checks that make it trustworthy and the questions it answers.

    g = Lineage.from_json(obj)          # full form {"artifacts": [...]} or the simple chain {"geometry": ..., ...}
    g.checks()                          # broken references, cycles, changed files, stale derivations, mixed revisions
    g.upstream("PRED-883")              # how was this produced?
    g.downstream("CAD-001")             # what depends on this (impact of a change)?
    g.to_prov()                         # W3C PROV-JSON

children.name: pinneapple_data.lineage.registry
children.doc:
One graph over the four registry stores (issue #156, phase 3 of the physical data graph).

``pinneapple_registry`` keeps problems, datasets, models and experiments in four stores that do not know about each
other: every record is filed under a ``problem_id`` and nothing points from a model back to the simulations it was
trained on. This module writes the edges the stores do record as one :class:`~pinneapple_data.lineage.graph.Lineage`,
so a prediction can be traced to the problem, the geometry, the simulation runs, the dataset and model versions and
the validation record that stand behind it.

Nothing is inferred that a store does not say. Which dataset a model was trained on is a free-form key in its
metadata (``datasets``, ``dataset``, ``scenarios``, ``trained_on``); when the key is absent the model is linked to the
problem it is filed under and to nothing else, the node says so, and ``Lineage.trace()`` reports the dataset as
missing. The same holds for the geometry and for the validation record: the answer says what was not recorded instead
of filling the hole.

    from pinneapple_registry import ArtifactRegistry
    from pinneapple_data.lineage import from_registry

    reg = ArtifactRegistry("artifacts")
    g = from_registry(reg, "poisson_2d", prediction="PRED-001")
    answer = g.trace("PRED-001")
    answer["missing"]                          # ['geometry'] when nobody recorded the geometry

functions.name: from_registry
functions.sig: (registry: Any, problem_id: str, *, prediction: str | None = None, model_version: str | None = None) -> Lineage
functions.doc:
Build the lineage of one problem from the four stores: the problem versions, the datasets (the simulation runs)
and the geometry they name, the model versions with the datasets and the run they came from, and the validation
record of each model version.

``registry`` is an ``ArtifactRegistry`` or the path of one. ``prediction`` adds a prediction node linked to
``model_version``, or to the newest stored model version when that is not given; ``trace()`` on it answers the
question of issue #156: problem, geometry, simulation runs, dataset version, model version and validation record.

children.summary: One graph over the four registry stores (issue #156, phase 3 of the physical data graph).

children.doc:

children.name: pinneapple_data.multifidelity
children.doc:
Multi-fidelity regression over a table: what the cheap model buys, and how much of the expensive one is enough.

A multi-fidelity study has two fidelities of the same designs -- a cheap model that runs everywhere and an expensive
one that ran on a few designs -- and one question: *how much does the cheap one buy?* This module answers it as a
learning curve: split the expensive designs into a training part of size N and the rest, fit the target four ways,
and score each way on the designs it did not see.

===================  ==============================================================================
``low_fidelity``     no fit at all: the cheap model's own value at that design. The baseline a learned
                     correction has to beat, and the reason a study like this is worth running.
``geometry``         a surrogate of the target from the design alone -- the answer to "what if there is no
                     cheap model".
``difference``       a surrogate of ``y_high - y_low`` from the design: the cheap model everywhere plus a
                     learned correction. This is the multi-fidelity model, and it is what a co-kriging
                     study computes in the two-fidelity case.
``residual_feature`` a surrogate of the same difference, with the cheap model's value at the design among
                     its inputs. When this beats ``difference`` the correction depends on *where* the cheap
                     model is, not only on *where* the design is.

What this module deliberately does not do: **pretrain a surrogate on the cheap fidelity**. The cheap model is a
function that is already available at every design, so a surrogate of it adds nothing but its own error -- what the
1024 cheap runs buy is the shape of the correction, and the ``difference`` row measures exactly that. (With a cheap
fidelity that is itself expensive to evaluate, pretraining would be the thing to do; this is not that case.)

    >>> from pinneapple_data.multifidelity import FidelityPair, learning_curve
    >>> pair = FidelityPair.pair(X_low, y_low, X_high, y_high)
    >>> curve = learning_curve(pair, budgets=(8, 16, 32))
    >>> print(curve.table())

The regressor is kernel ridge with an RBF kernel, in closed form: no epochs, no seed noise beyond the split, and it
behaves at N = 8, where a neural network has nothing to learn from. A row of the curve is a median over repeated
random splits, with the interval the medians of the repeats span.

classes.name: FidelityPair
classes.doc:
Two fidelities of the same design space.

``low_at_high`` is the cheap model evaluated at the expensive designs. It is not optional and it is not
interpolated here: a study whose cheap model cannot be evaluated where the expensive one ran is not a
multi-fidelity study, it is two unrelated datasets, and guessing the value would make every number below a guess
too.

methods.name: pair
methods.sig: (design_low, values_low, design_high, values_high, *, atol: float = 1e-09) -> FidelityPair
methods.doc:
The pair, with the cheap model evaluated at each expensive design by finding that design among the cheap
ones.

classes.name: KernelRidge
classes.doc:
Kernel ridge regression with an RBF kernel, in closed form.

The length scale is the median pairwise distance of the training designs -- a standard heuristic that needs no
tuning, which matters at eight training points. ``scale`` divides the inputs first, so a design in metres and a
Mach number are compared on the same footing: the caller passes the span of each input, or leaves it as the
training range, which is the same thing when the training points cover the space.

classes.name: LearningCurve
classes.doc: Every row of the curve, and the splits behind them.

methods.name: spread
methods.doc: The worst and the best of the repeats -- the spread of the seeds, not a confidence interval of the mean.

classes.name: FieldPair
classes.doc:
Two fidelities of a *field* over one shared discretisation.

Every expensive run's field lives on the same nodes as its cheap run's -- that is what makes the difference a
subtraction and not an interpolation, and it is stated here as a requirement rather than hoped for. ``position``
is whatever orders the nodes along the surface (an arc length, a coordinate); it is not used by the curve, only
reported with it, because a field model that reads the position is a different model.

methods.name: run_scale
methods.doc: The magnitude of each run's cheap field, ``(n_high,)``.

functions.name: relative_l2
functions.doc: ``||prediction - measured|| / ||measured||`` over the rows -- the form a physical target is scored in.

functions.name: r2
functions.doc: The coefficient of determination; zero for the mean, negative for worse than it.

functions.name: learning_curve
functions.sig: (pair: FidelityPair, *, budgets = (4, 8, 16, 32), repeats: int = 10, seed: int = 0, ridge: float = 1e-08, strategies = STRATEGIES) -> LearningCurve
functions.doc:
Fit each strategy on N expensive designs and score it on the ones it did not see.

For ``N < n_high`` the split is a random ``N`` of the expensive designs (``repeats`` times, one seed), and the
score is on the remaining ones. For ``N == n_high`` there is nothing left to hold out, so each design is predicted
from the other ``N - 1`` (leave-one-out) -- a different question, said so in the row, and the only honest way to
put the full budget on the same axis.

Every strategy is scored on the *same* held-out designs of a repeat, so the comparison between them is paired.
The scales of the inputs and of the cheap model are the pair's own, so a design in metres and one in Mach number
are on the same footing.

functions.name: residual_rank
functions.sig: (residual: np.ndarray, *, components: int = 1, scale: np.ndarray | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
How much of the residual field a rank-``k`` model of the runs captures.

The residual of a run is one vector over the nodes. Stacked over runs, its singular value decomposition says how
many independent *shapes* of correction there are: if the first mode carries most of the energy, the correction is
one profile with an amplitude per design, and a study of it is a study of that amplitude.

``scale`` divides each run's residual by a per-run magnitude first. On the capsule corpus the energy share comes
out about the same either way (80 % raw against 81 % normalised), but the *coefficients* do not: raw, they span
the 175x the heating spans, and no regression on six inputs learns that. Pass the norm of each run's own field
(what :meth:`FieldPair.run_scale` returns) to measure the structure of the relative correction.

functions.name: field_learning_curve
functions.sig: (pair: FieldPair, *, budgets = (8, 16, 32), repeats: int = 10, seed: int = 0, components: int = 2, ridge: float = 1e-08, strategies = FIELD_STRATEGIES) -> LearningCurve
functions.doc:
The learning curve of a field, with a low-rank correction instead of a network per node.

==================  ==============================================================================
``low_fidelity``    the cheap field itself, on the same nodes.
``mean_correction`` the cheap field plus the average *relative* residual of the training runs: one shape,
                    scaled by the run's own magnitude, and no dependence on the design. What a correction
                    buys when nothing is learned from the inputs.
``pod_correction``  the cheap field plus ``components`` relative residual modes, each amplitude learned from
                    the design by kernel ridge. The proper orthogonal decomposition of the residual with a
                    regression on its coefficients, which is the field analogue of ``difference``.

The correction is modelled **relative to each run's own magnitude** (:meth:`FieldPair.run_scale`) and then scaled
back by the cheap run's magnitude, which is known at every design because the cheap model runs everywhere. The
normalisation is not cosmetic: the heat flux spans 175x across designs in the capsule corpus, so the coefficients
of the raw decomposition span 175x too, and a regression on six inputs cannot learn a quantity whose scale is set
by the design. Normalised, the first mode carries 81 % of the residual energy and the third 97 %, and the
coefficients are O(0.1) for every run -- which is what makes them predictable at all.

Why low rank rather than a pointwise network: with a handful of expensive runs there are thousands of nodes and
only N fields, so a model free to choose every node's correction is fitting noise -- and the residual of a family
of shapes turns out to be a couple of modes deep, which :func:`residual_rank` measures instead of assuming. The
score is the relative L2 over each held-out run's whole field, then the median over runs and splits.

children.summary: Multi-fidelity regression over a table: what the cheap model buys, and how much of the expensive one is enough.

children.name: pinneapple_data.noether_dataset
children.doc:
Noether ↔ PINNeAPPle data bridge.

Provides two adapters:

NoetherDatasetBridge
    Wraps a ``noether.data.base.Dataset`` (or any mapping-style dataset
    that yields ``{field: tensor}`` dicts) so it can be used as a standard
    ``torch.utils.data.Dataset`` inside PINNeAPPle's training loops.

PhysicalSampleDataset
    Converts a list of PINNeAPPle ``PhysicalSample`` (UPD format) objects
    into a Noether-compatible ``{field: tensor}`` dataset, enabling the full
    Noether training pipeline (``WeightedLossTrainer``, ``noether-train``)
    to consume data generated by PINNeAPPle's simulation modules.

Workflow examples
-----------------
# 1. Feed Noether built-in dataset to PINNeAPPle Trainer
>>> from noether.data.datasets import DrivAerMLDataset
>>> from pinneapple_data.noether_dataset import NoetherDatasetBridge
>>> noether_ds = DrivAerMLDataset(root="/data/driveaerml")
>>> bridge = NoetherDatasetBridge(noether_ds, target_fields=["pressure", "velocity"])
>>> # Use bridge with any PINNeAPPle DataLoader

# 2. Feed PINNeAPPle simulation data to NoetherSurrogateTrainer
>>> from pinneapple_data.noether_dataset import PhysicalSampleDataset
>>> samples = [...]  # list of PhysicalSample from MuJoCoRunner / GenesisRunner / FEniCS
>>> ds = PhysicalSampleDataset(samples, input_fields=["qpos","qvel"], output_fields=["xpos"])
>>> loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(ds, batch_size=8, shuffle=True)

classes.name: NoetherDatasetBridge
classes.sig: (noether_dataset, input_fields: Optional[List[str]] = None, target_fields: Optional[List[str]] = None, transform = None, device: Optional[str] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Bridge a ``noether.data.base.Dataset`` to a plain PyTorch Dataset.

Makes Noether's built-in datasets (DrivAerML, AhmedML, SIMSHIFT, etc.)
usable in PINNeAPPle training loops without any Hydra/config machinery.

Parameters
----------
noether_dataset : a Noether Dataset instance
input_fields : field names to expose as model inputs.
    If None, all non-target fields are treated as inputs.
target_fields : field names to expose as targets (suffixed with ``_target``
    in the output dict for consistency with ``NoetherSurrogateTrainer``).
    If None, no target separation is applied.
transform : optional callable applied to each sample dict after retrieval.
device : move tensors to this device. None = keep on CPU.

classes.name: PhysicalSampleDataset
classes.sig: (samples: Sequence, input_fields: Optional[List[str]] = None, output_fields: Optional[List[str]] = None, include_coords: bool = False, transform = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Convert a list of PINNeAPPle ``PhysicalSample`` (UPD) to a
Noether-compatible ``{field: tensor}`` PyTorch Dataset.

Each sample in the list becomes one dataset item. Fields from
``PhysicalSample.fields`` are exposed; coordinate arrays from
``PhysicalSample.coords`` are optionally included.

Parameters
----------
samples : list of PhysicalSample
input_fields : field names from ``PhysicalSample.fields`` to use as
    model inputs. If None, all fields except output_fields are used.
output_fields : field names used as supervision targets (suffixed with
    ``_target`` in the output dict).
include_coords : if True, include coordinate arrays as extra input fields.
transform : optional callable applied to each sample dict.

methods.name: from_upd_list
methods.sig: (samples: Sequence, input_fields: Optional[List[str]] = None, output_fields: Optional[List[str]] = None, include_coords: bool = False) -> 'PhysicalSampleDataset'
methods.doc: Convenience constructor — alias for the standard ``__init__``.

functions.name: split_physical_samples
functions.sig: (samples: Sequence, val_fraction: float = 0.1, seed: int = 42, **dataset_kwargs) -> tuple['PhysicalSampleDataset', 'PhysicalSampleDataset']
functions.doc:
Split a list of PhysicalSamples into train and validation datasets.

Parameters
----------
samples : full list of PhysicalSample
val_fraction : fraction reserved for validation (0 < val_fraction < 1)
seed : random seed for reproducibility
**dataset_kwargs : forwarded to ``PhysicalSampleDataset``

Returns
-------
(train_dataset, val_dataset)

children.summary: Noether ↔ PINNeAPPle data bridge.

children.name: pinneapple_data.parameter_sampling
children.doc:
Design-of-experiments parameter-space sampling.

Generic helpers for sampling a bounded parameter space — e.g. to build a
synthetic dataset by sweeping a physical problem's parameters, or to run a
global sensitivity analysis. Distinct from `collocation.py`/`active_learning.py`
in this package, which sample *collocation points in the PDE domain*; this
module samples *parameter values* (physical constants, boundary condition
magnitudes, geometry dimensions, etc.).

Built on `scipy.stats.qmc` — no extra dependency beyond scipy.

functions.name: sample_parameters
functions.sig: (param_ranges: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], n_samples: int, method: SamplingMethod = 'lhs', seed: int = 0) -> list[dict[str, float]]
functions.doc:
Sample `n_samples` points from a bounded parameter space.

Parameters
----------
param_ranges : {name: (low, high)} for each parameter to sample.
n_samples : number of samples to draw.
method : "lhs" (Latin Hypercube, default — good space-filling for a
    moderate sample budget), "sobol" (low-discrepancy sequence, best for
    large sample counts / convergence studies), "random" (plain uniform),
    or "grid" (regular grid, exponential in dimension — use only for
    low-dimensional sweeps).
seed : RNG seed for reproducibility.

Returns
-------
A list of `n_samples` dicts, one key per `param_ranges` entry.

functions.name: saltelli_perturbation_sweep
functions.sig: (nominal: dict[str, float], param_ranges: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], n_base: int = 8, seed: int = 0) -> list[dict[str, float]]
functions.doc:
Build a Saltelli-style sample set for first-order/total-order Sobol
global sensitivity analysis, without requiring the SALib dependency.

Produces 2*n_base_rounded*(d+2)-ish samples: a base matrix A, a
resampling matrix B, and d "swap one column of A with B" matrices —
the standard construction needed to estimate first-order and total-order
Sobol indices from model evaluations on this sample set.

`nominal` is accepted for interface symmetry with call sites that also
need a baseline point, but is not itself perturbed here — sensitivity
indices are computed downstream from model outputs on the returned
sample set, not from this function.

children.summary: Design-of-experiments parameter-space sampling.

classes.name: PhysicalSample
classes.doc:
Unified Physical Sample (UPD-aligned) used across Pinneapple.

This structure serves as a standardized container for physical data
used in modeling, simulation, and PINN training workflows.

Attributes
----------
state : xr.Dataset or Dict[str, Any]
    Core physical state representation. Preferably an xarray.Dataset
    for structured grid data, or a dict-like structure for other formats.
geometry : Optional[Any]
    Optional geometry asset describing spatial structure.
schema : Dict[str, Any]
    Governing equations, boundary/initial conditions, forcing terms,
    unit policies, and related metadata.
domain : Dict[str, Any]
    Domain interpretation metadata (grid, mesh, graph, points, etc.).
provenance : Dict[str, Any]
    Lineage metadata including identifiers, source, tiling,
    time span, and other traceability information.
extras : Dict[str, Any]
    Extensible container for additional artifacts such as
    feature caches, mesh labels, SDFs, etc.

methods.name: domain_type
methods.doc: Infer the domain type of this sample.

methods.name: is_grid
methods.doc: Check if the sample represents structured grid data.

methods.name: is_mesh
methods.doc: Check if the sample represents mesh-based data.

methods.name: is_graph
methods.doc: Check if the sample represents graph-based data.

methods.name: list_variables
methods.doc: List available physical variables in the state.

methods.name: summary
methods.doc: Generate a structured summary of this PhysicalSample.

methods.name: to_train_dict
methods.sig: (*, x_vars: Iterable[str], y_vars: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None, coords: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None, time_dim: Optional[str] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Convert this PhysicalSample into a canonical training dictionary.

children.name: pinneapple_data.physical_units
children.doc:
Physical units and quantities for engineering data (PINNeAPPle Physical Data Layer).

Dependency-free (standard library only) so that data tools can use it without the
training stack. It answers three questions about a column of engineering data:

1. **What unit is it in?** ``split_header("T_supply [°C]") -> ("T_supply", "°C")`` and
   ``parse_unit("kg/(m·s)")`` turn header text into a :class:`Unit` with an SI factor,
   an offset (temperatures only) and a dimension vector.
2. **What physical quantity is it?** ``infer_quantity(name, unit)`` combines the unit's
   dimension with keywords in the name (pressure and stress share a dimension; the name
   decides) and returns a :class:`QuantityGuess` with a confidence and the reason.
3. **Is a value physically possible?** Every quantity in :data:`QUANTITIES` carries hard
   limits (impossible values, e.g. an absolute temperature below 0 K) and a typical
   engineering range (suspicious values), both in SI.

Conversions are exact definitions where they exist (NIST SP 811, Appendix B).
Temperature *differences* are not distinguished from temperatures: a column of
"ΔT [°F]" converts with the absolute-temperature offset. :func:`convert` therefore takes
``difference=True`` for those columns, and :func:`infer_quantity` flags names with
"delta"/"diff"/"Δ".

classes.name: Unit
classes.doc: A unit: ``SI value = value * factor + offset``.

classes.name: UnitError
classes.doc:
A unit this library cannot work with. ``fix`` (when given) is the action the user can take, rendered as a
second line the same way ``pinneapple_core.errors`` renders it -- kept here, without importing that package, so
the lowest layer of the library carries no dependency on the one above it.

functions.name: parse_unit
functions.doc:
Parse a unit expression: ``°C``, ``kg/m^3``, ``W/(m·K)``, ``m³/h``, ``N*m``, ``psig``.

Raises :class:`UnitError` if any token is unknown.

functions.name: convert
functions.sig: (values, src: str, dst: str, difference: bool = False)
functions.doc: Convert values (scalar or numpy array) from ``src`` to ``dst``.

functions.name: split_header
functions.doc:
Split a column header into (name, unit text). ``"T_supply [°C]"`` -> ``("T_supply", "°C")``;
also understands ``Pressure (bar)``, ``flow, m3/h``, ``power in kW`` and suffixes like
``T_inlet_degC``, ``pressure_bar`` or ``vibration_mm_s``. Returns ``(header, None)`` when no
unit is found. A short suffix (``_C``, ``_A``) counts as a unit only when the rest of the name
names a matching quantity (``T_out_C`` yes, ``Line_A`` no).

functions.name: infer_quantity
functions.doc: Infer the physical quantity of a column from its unit dimension and name keywords.

children.summary: Physical units and quantities for engineering data (PINNeAPPle Physical Data Layer).

children.name: pinneapple_data.physics_case
children.doc:
``PhysicsCase`` -- a minimal bridge between the three disjoint "partial
canonical representations" of a physics problem already in this repo:

1. Geometry/mesh objects (``MeshData``, a trimesh mesh, a voxel grid, ...)
   produced by ``pinneapple_design.geometry`` and its ``io`` bridges.
2. ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.ProblemSpec`` -- the PDE/BC/IC
   *definition* of a physics problem, built by ``ProblemBuilder``
   (``pinneapple_physics/pde_environment/builder.py``).
3. ``pinneapple_data`` UPD-family *results* objects (e.g. ``PhysicalSample``
   from ``pinneapple_data.physical_sample``, or whatever a format reader
   such as ``meshio_to_upd``/``cgns_to_upd`` hands back) once a case has
   actually been run.

Separately, ``pinneapple_pdb.benchmarks.BenchmarkEntry`` is a fourth, even
narrower thing: a named *reference* dataset used to sanity-check results.

None of the above know about each other. ``PhysicsCase`` does not redefine
or replace any of them -- it is a single dataclass that *references* the
real objects (geometry, a real ``ProblemSpec``, a solver name/config, a
real UPD-family results object, and a benchmark name) so a whole physics
case can be constructed, passed around, and (once results exist) checked
against a named benchmark as one unit, instead of the caller manually
keeping four disconnected variables in sync.

Deliberately NOT included: a registry, a fluent builder, or a plugin
system for any of the three underlying representations -- those already
exist (``ProblemBuilder``, ``SolverRegistry``, ``pinneapple_pdb.benchmarks``
itself) and this module only points at them.

classes.name: BenchmarkComparison
classes.doc:
Plain numeric comparison produced by
``PhysicsCase.validate_against_benchmark()``.

This intentionally stops at numbers, not a verdict: whether a given
RMSE/relative error counts as "passing" is a policy decision that
already lives in ``pinneapple_analysis/verification`` and
``pinneapple_llm.guardrail.PhysicsGuardrail`` (see
``PhysicsGuardrail._check_reference`` for the thresholded version of
this same comparison) -- duplicating that judgment here would make
this module the "new validation engine" it is explicitly scoped not
to be.

classes.name: PhysicsCase
classes.doc:
One physics case: geometry + physics spec + solver choice + results,
referenced together.

Every field is optional -- a case may be defined before geometry
exists, before it has been assigned a solver, or before it has been
run at all. Nothing here is copied or redefined: ``physics`` is a
direct reference to a real ``ProblemSpec``, ``results`` is a direct
reference to a real UPD-family object (e.g. ``PhysicalSample``, or
whatever ``meshio_to_upd``/``cgns_to_upd``/... produced), and
``geometry`` is a direct reference to whatever the geometry-io layer
already produces (``MeshData``, a trimesh object, a voxel grid, ...).

Attributes
----------
name : short human-readable identifier for this case (not required to
    match ``physics.name``/``problem_id``, since a case may exist
    before ``physics`` is set).
geometry : reference to a geometry/mesh object, or ``None``.
geometry_kind : disambiguation tag for ``geometry``, e.g. "mesh",
    "voxel", "cad", "points" -- free-form, not a registry key.
physics : a real ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.ProblemSpec``,
    or ``None`` if the physics has not been specified yet.
solver : name of the intended solver/backend, expected to match a
    ``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.registry.SolverRegistry``
    entry (e.g. "lbm", "fem", "fvm", "openfoam", "sph", ...) -- this
    module does not validate against the registry (that would add an
    import-time dependency on every solver backend); it is just a
    name.
solver_config : kwargs for that solver, or ``None``.
results : reference to a UPD-family object once this case has been
    run (e.g. a ``pinneapple_data.physical_sample.PhysicalSample``, or
    another UPD-shaped object), or ``None`` before it has been run.
reference_benchmark : a name resolvable via
    ``pinneapple_pdb.benchmarks.get_benchmark()``, or ``None``.
metadata : free-form provenance dict. Mirrors the
    ``provenance``/``schema`` dict convention already used by
    ``pinneapple_data.physical_sample.PhysicalSample`` (plain
    ``Dict[str, Any]``, no fixed schema beyond convention) rather than
    inventing a new provenance shape.

methods.name: validate_against_benchmark
methods.doc: Compare ``self.results`` against ``self.reference_benchmark``.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc:
Serialize this case to a plain ``dict``, following the same
``dataclasses.asdict``-based convention already used elsewhere in
``pinneapple_data`` (see ``pinneapple_data.zarr_store``).

methods.name: from_dict
methods.doc:
Reconstruct a ``PhysicsCase`` from a dict produced by
``to_dict()``.

children.summary: PhysicsCase -- a minimal bridge between the three disjoint "partial canonical representations" of a physics problem already in this repo: 1.

children.name: pinneapple_data.prefetch_adaptive
children.doc: Adaptive prefetch IterableDataset for Zarr-backed UPD stores with configurable queue control.

classes.name: AdaptivePrefetchConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for adaptive prefetching behavior.

This config controls:
  - The maximum queue capacity used for prefetch buffering.
  - An adaptive target fill level (within bounds) used by a producer thread
    to regulate how many prefetched samples to keep buffered.
  - A control loop that adjusts the target fill based on queue occupancy.
  - Optional pinning and device transfer behaviors.

Attributes
----------
queue_max : int
    Hard maximum capacity of the prefetch queue.
min_target_fill : int
    Minimum allowed adaptive target fill level.
max_target_fill : int
    Maximum allowed adaptive target fill level.
target_fill_init : int
    Initial target fill level used before the controller adapts it.
control_period_s : float
    Period (seconds) for the controller to evaluate queue occupancy.
increase_step : int
    Step size used to increase the target fill when queue is frequently drained.
decrease_step : int
    Step size used to decrease the target fill when queue stays near full.
high_watermark : float
    Occupancy ratio threshold (qsize / queue_max) above which target fill decreases.
low_watermark : float
    Occupancy ratio threshold below which target fill increases.
use_sample_cache : bool
    Whether to enable per-sample caching at the store level.
pin_memory : bool
    Whether to pin sample tensors in CPU pinned memory after reading.
target_device : str
    Desired device for yielded samples ("cpu" or "cuda...").
transfer_non_blocking : bool
    Whether GPU transfers should be non-blocking when supported.

classes.name: AdaptivePrefetchZarrUPDIterable
classes.sig: (root: str, *, fields: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, coords: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, dtype: Optional[torch.dtype] = None, start: int = 0, end: Optional[int] = None, stride: int = 1, sample_ctor: Any = None, cache: Optional[ZarrByteCacheConfig] = None, cfg: Optional[AdaptivePrefetchConfig] = None)
classes.doc:
IterableDataset that streams samples from a cached Zarr-backed UPD store
with adaptive prefetching.

Prefetching model
-----------------
- A bounded queue buffers prefetched samples (hard capacity = cfg.queue_max).
- A producer thread reads samples and pushes them to the queue.
- A controller thread periodically adjusts a shared `target_fill` value
  within [cfg.min_target_fill, cfg.max_target_fill], based on queue occupancy:
    * If occupancy > cfg.high_watermark: decrease target fill.
    * If occupancy < cfg.low_watermark: increase target fill.
- The producer throttles itself to keep the queue size below `target_fill`.

Multi-worker behavior
---------------------
When used with a PyTorch DataLoader with multiple workers, each worker process:
- Builds its own store instance and its own producer/controller threads.
- Receives a disjoint subset of indices based on worker_id and stride.

Device behavior
---------------
- Samples are read on CPU.
- If cfg.pin_memory is True, tensor fields/coords are pinned.
- If cfg.target_device starts with "cuda", samples are moved to GPU before yield.

children.summary: Adaptive prefetch IterableDataset for Zarr-backed UPD stores with configurable queue control.

children.name: pinneapple_data.preflight
pinneapple_data.preflight.calculix
children.doc:
Pre-flight rules for CalculiX (and flat Abaqus) input decks: mesh, sections and materials, the properties each
procedure needs, unit consistency, supports and loads, initial conditions and step settings.

children.name: pinneapple_data.preflight.limits
children.doc:
The known numerical limits of the OpenFOAM connectors, each with the case that demonstrates it (issue #132).

Three solvers hit real limits in earlier case campaigns — ``buoyantSimpleFoam``, ``buoyantPimpleFoam`` and free-surface
flow with k-omega SST — and "it failed once" is not something a connector can act on. This module records, per
solver, **the decision** (accepted and documented, worked around, or unsupported), **what was measured**, and **the
minimal case that demonstrates it**, so the connector's rules (:mod:`pinneapple_data.preflight.openfoam`) cite
evidence instead of folklore.

Every entry below was measured on OpenFOAM v2606 (macOS arm64, native build) on 2026-11-24, with the cases of
``tests/test_openfoam_limits.py``: ``buoyant_simple_cavity`` (a 20x20x1 closed cavity, hot left wall at 350 K, cold
right wall at 300 K, k-omega SST, 300 SIMPLE iterations, 0.57 s of solver time), ``buoyant_pimple_room`` (the
shipped ``hotRoom`` tutorial cut to endTime 20 s, ten PIMPLE steps, 2.1 s), and ``dambreak_sst`` (the shipped
``interFoam/RAS/damBreak`` case switched from kEpsilon to kOmegaSST, 71 steps to 0.2 s, 1.05 s). The verbatim log line
of each failure is in ``detail``.

The three decisions
-------------------
``buoyantSimpleFoam`` — **accepted, with two hard requirements the connector enforces**: ``constant/g`` and
``pRefCell``/``pRefPoint``. Both missing cases are a fatal stop at start-up, not a divergence, so a case either has
them or never runs. Relaxation is a quality issue, not a fatal one, and is documented as such.

``buoyantPimpleFoam`` — **accepted, with the start-up flux correction required**: the transient compressible solver
needs a ``rho`` linear-solver entry (fatal without it) and ``correctPhi yes`` with a ``pcorr`` solver. Without the
correction the run still completes, silently, with a first-step local continuity error 12 times larger (measured
1.6e-3 against 1.3e-4); that is the kind of wrong answer a campaign must not accept, so the connector warns.

``interIsoFoam`` + k-omega SST — **supported, and run for real**: the free-surface case that had never been run
completed its 71 steps with the interface bounded (min -7.7e-5, max 1.0005 on the water fraction) and a maximum
Courant number of 1.02. The cost is three dictionary entries that kEpsilon did not need (``wallDist`` in fvSchemes,
``div(rhoPhi,omega)``, and an ``omega``/``omegaFinal`` solver entry), each of which is a fatal stop if missing — so the
connector checks them instead of leaving a model switch to discover them at run time. The known limit that remains
is documented rather than solved: turbulence in the gas phase has no physical scale to calibrate against, so the
fields it produces in air are numerical, and the decision is to accept that and say so.

children.name: pinneapple_data.process_optimizer
children.doc:
Data-driven process optimization for industrial plants (plain machine learning, no physics model).

From historical operating data:

1. **Clean** with the data-health report: duplicate timestamps dropped, error codes, impossible values,
   stuck-sensor and spike spans set to missing (:func:`clean_for_modeling`).
2. **Learn** the plant: a gradient-boosting model (scikit-learn ``HistGradientBoostingRegressor``) predicts
   the KPI (e.g. plant power) from the *levers* the operator controls (setpoints, speeds) and the *context*
   the operator does not (weather, load). It is scored on the most recent 20-30 % of the record, which it
   never saw (time split, no shuffling). Its L2 regularisation is chosen by forward-chaining time-series
   cross-validation inside the training part, and the per-fold errors are reported.
3. **Optimize** each test-period hour: try lever combinations and keep the one with the best predicted
   KPI that also
   * stays inside the operating envelope: the lever + context combination must resemble situations in
     the data (nearest-neighbour distance), because the model cannot know what it has never seen;
   * respects constraints on other measured outputs (e.g. CHW return temperature <= 13 C), each with its own
     model;
   * moves each lever at most a set fraction of its range from the current value (gradual change).
4. **Report** the predicted saving with a range from an ensemble of bootstrapped models, the recommended
   setpoint schedule against the most influential context variable, partial-dependence curves and
   feature importance.

The saving is a model estimate from correlations in historical data, not a guarantee: the right next step
is a supervised trial (A/B by day). The built-in example (:func:`example_plant_operations`) is a simulated
chilled-water plant whose true physics is known, so the predicted saving can be checked against the true one.

functions.name: suggest_roles
functions.doc: Guess target / levers / context from column names (to be reviewed by a person).

functions.name: clean_for_modeling
functions.sig: (df: pd.DataFrame, report: Dict[str, Any]) -> Tuple[pd.DataFrame, List[str]]
functions.doc: Time-sorted numeric table with the problems found by the health report set to missing.

functions.name: time_series_cv
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, n_folds: int = 4, l2_grid: Sequence[float] = L2_GRID, seed: int = 0) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Forward-chaining cross-validation on the training period: fold k trains on the first k blocks and is scored
on the next one (never on the past), for every L2 regularisation strength in ``l2_grid``. Picks the strength
with the lowest mean validation MAE; the per-fold errors show how stable the model is over time.

children.name: pinneapple_data.provenance
children.doc:
Provenance: the minimum a dataset, a run or a model must record to be reproducible, and the validator (#39).

A dataset, an experiment result and a model card are all claims of the form "these numbers came from this physics,
computed this way". Without a record of *what* computed them, *which* code was running, *which* randomness was in
play and *which* exact bytes went in, the claim cannot be re-derived -- and neither a reviewer nor the person who
wrote it six months earlier can tell whether a number that looks wrong is a bug or a different case.

The minimum, and why each field is there:

===================  ==========================================================================
``solver``           what produced the numbers (``"openfoam-simplefoam"``, ``"pinn"``, ``"closed-form"``)
``library_version``  which PINNeAPPle computed them (a released version is a reproducible reference)
``seed``             which randomness was in play -- an integer, or ``"deterministic"`` for a solver
                     that has none (steady RANS, closed form, FEM assembly)
``data_hash``        a way back to the exact inputs: the SHA-256 of the input file(s), or of the
                     canonical bytes of a synthetic problem
``commit``           which code was running, when the record was produced from a checkout (a
                     released ``library_version`` and a ``commit`` are both references to code; at
                     least the version is mandatory, and this is recorded whenever it is knowable)
===================  ==========================================================================

A mesh-based solver additionally records ``mesh`` (cells or nodes, and the hash of the mesh file): a case that ran
on "the mesh" and does not say which one is not reproducible even with everything else.

Usage::

    from pinneapple_data.provenance import build_provenance, require

    record = build_provenance("openfoam-simplefoam", seed="deterministic", data_hash_of="case/0/U", mesh={"cells": 1_200_000})
    require(record)                     # raises ValueError listing exactly what is missing

``scripts/validate_provenance.py`` runs the same check over every model card and dataset in the tree, so a
repository that gains an artifact without provenance fails a job rather than looking complete.

functions.name: library_version
functions.doc: The version of PINNeAPPle in this interpreter (``""`` if it cannot be determined).

functions.name: git_commit
functions.doc:
The commit of the checkout that contains ``path`` (default: this file), or ``""`` outside a git tree.

``PINNEAPPLE_COMMIT`` wins when it is set: a container or a CI runner that knows the commit (and strips
``.git``) records it that way, which is the case the environment variable exists for.

functions.name: data_hash
functions.doc: SHA-256 of a file, in the form the records carry (``"sha256:<hex>"``).

functions.name: data_hash_of_bytes
functions.doc: SHA-256 of the canonical bytes of a synthetic input (a problem description, an array), same form.

functions.name: solver_uses_a_mesh
functions.doc: Whether ``solver`` is one of the mesh-based ones (:data:`MESH_SOLVERS`), by name prefix.

functions.name: problems
functions.sig: (record: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]], *, uses_a_mesh: Optional[bool] = None) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
What is missing from a provenance ``record``, one readable line each (empty list = complete).

``uses_a_mesh`` overrides the guess from the solver name: a record for a solver this module does not know can
still declare that the answer depends on the mesh.

functions.name: require
functions.sig: (record: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]], *, uses_a_mesh: Optional[bool] = None) -> Mapping[str, Any]
functions.doc: ``record`` if it is complete, else ``ValueError`` listing what is missing and how to fill it (issue #39).

functions.name: build_provenance
functions.sig: (solver: str, *, seed: int | str, data_hash: str = '', data_hash_of: str | Path | None = None, mesh: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None, commit: Optional[str] = None, version: Optional[str] = None, **extra) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A complete provenance record, filling in what can be determined: version, commit, the hash of a file.

``data_hash_of`` hashes a path; ``data_hash`` takes a hash the caller already computed. ``commit=None`` looks
for ``PINNEAPPLE_COMMIT`` and then the enclosing checkout (``commit=""`` states that it is not knowable, which
:func:`problems` will report). Extra keyword arguments are recorded as they are (``app``, ``study_id``,
``source``, ...).

children.name: pinneapple_data.readiness
children.doc:
Data readiness: may this dataset start a training run? (#1491, part of #1497)

Between "the company has engineering data" and "a model trains on it" the library had nothing: ``Trainer`` trained on
whatever arrays it was given, and the checks that existed (``data_health``, ``cae.quality``, ``preflight``,
``pinneapple_veriphysics``) did not gate anything. This module is that stage.

It **composes**, it does not re-implement:

| group | where the checking happens |
|---|---|
| ``schema`` | the dataset manifest itself: required fields, columns, roles, files that exist |
| ``units`` | :mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`, plus the declared units against the ones in the table header |
| ``conditions`` | the manifest: every output field has at least one boundary or initial condition behind it |
| ``validity`` | the manifest: the operating point inside the range the data is declared to cover |
| ``table`` | :func:`pinneapple_data.data_health.analyze` |
| ``case`` | :func:`pinneapple_data.preflight.preflight` |

The verdict is **not a function of the score**. ``status`` comes from the severities (one critical finding is ``FAIL``,
whatever the score is); the score is reported next to it, with the formula in the report, because a number next to a
verdict is useful and a number *as* a verdict is how a critical units mismatch becomes "87 %, ship it".

:func:`require` is the gate. ``FAIL`` and ``NOT_ASSESSED`` always stop a run; ``WARNING`` stops it unless a review
record (:mod:`pinneapple_data.review`, #1493) accepts exactly those findings for exactly this dataset digest.
Behaviour without a report is unchanged -- nothing that exists today starts failing.

The dataset manifest (``pinneapple.readiness.dataset/1``)::

    {"schema": "pinneapple.readiness.dataset/1",
     "name": "plate_sweep", "version": "1.0",
     "columns": [{"name": "Re", "role": "input", "unit": "1"},
                 {"name": "delta_p", "role": "output", "unit": "Pa"}],
     "boundary_conditions": [{"field": "delta_p", "kind": "dirichlet", "value": 0}],
     "validity": {"Re": [1.0e4, 1.0e5]},
     "operating_point": {"Re": 5.0e4}}

classes.name: ReadinessError
classes.sig: (message: str, *, report: Optional['ReadinessReport'] = None, findings: Sequence['Finding'] = (), review: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None) -> None
classes.doc: Training was refused. ``findings`` holds what stopped it; the message names ids, evidence and fixes.

classes.name: Finding
classes.doc: One problem, in the shape the sibling reports use: id, group, severity, what, evidence, and the fix.

classes.name: ReadinessPolicy
classes.doc:
Which findings are critical, which groups apply, and where the policy came from.

The default policy is the library's: the checks that make a dataset unusable (a missing unit, a missing boundary
condition, an operating point outside the declared validity) are critical, and everything else is a warning.

methods.name: severity_of
methods.doc: The policy has the last word on how serious a finding is, then the check itself.

classes.name: ReadinessReport
classes.doc: The verdict, why, and the evidence behind it -- JSON-ready and renderable without the app.

methods.name: explain
methods.doc: The refusal in the words a user needs: ids, evidence and fix, one finding per line.

functions.name: digest_of
functions.sig: (subject: Any, files: Optional[Mapping[str, bytes]] = None) -> str
functions.doc:
``sha256:`` of the dataset description and, when there are files, of their contents.

The digest is what a review is tied to: change the dataset and the approval no longer applies (#1491, #1493).

functions.name: readiness
functions.sig: (subject: Any, *, policy: Optional[ReadinessPolicy] = None, table: Any = None, case_files: Optional[Mapping[str, bytes]] = None, base: Optional[str | Path] = None, name: str = '') -> ReadinessReport
functions.doc:
Assess a dataset and return the report. ``subject`` is a manifest (mapping or JSON path) or a table.

``table`` attaches the data itself (a DataFrame or a CSV/Excel path) so the table group runs; ``case_files``
attaches a solver case (``{filename: bytes}``) so the case group runs. Nothing is invented: a group that has no
input does not run, and a report with no group at all is ``NOT_ASSESSED``, never ``PASS``.

functions.name: require
functions.doc:
The gate: raise :class:`ReadinessError` unless this dataset may start a training run.

``review`` is a :class:`pinneapple_data.review.ReviewStore`; it is what turns a ``WARNING`` into a run, by
accepting exactly those findings for exactly this digest. ``FAIL`` and ``NOT_ASSESSED`` are never overridable.

children.name: pinneapple_data.regimes
children.doc:
Which physical regimes a dataset covers, and which ones it is missing (#171).

An audit that measures coverage of the *design space* answers "are these samples spread out?". It does not answer
"is there any turbulent case in here?", and that is the question a model answers wrongly: a surrogate trained on
laminar pipe flow and asked about a turbulent one is not interpolating, it is extrapolating with confidence.

A regime is a band of one dimensionless number, so the labels come from a number that already carries the physics —
Reynolds, Mach, Prandtl — and not from a cluster the data happened to form:

    >>> from pinneapple_data.regimes import PRESETS, regime_coverage
    >>> cov = regime_coverage([1200, 1800, 9500], PRESETS["reynolds_pipe"])   # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> cov.counts, cov.missing                                              # doctest: +SKIP
    ({'laminar': 2, 'transitional': 0, 'turbulent': 1}, ['transitional'])

`missing_regions()` turns each empty band back into the interval it covers, which is what a sampler needs to fill it:
the audit says what is missing, and the same object says where to look.

classes.name: Band
classes.doc: One regime: ``label`` for ``low <= value < high``; ``None`` means unbounded on that side.

classes.name: RegimeSpec
classes.doc:
The bands of one dimensionless number, in order, with no gap between them.

The bands have to tile the line: a sample that falls in no band is a hole in the spec, not a regime of its own, and
the constructor refuses it instead of returning "unknown" for a value that is perfectly well defined.

methods.name: label
methods.doc: The band a value falls in; ``"missing"`` for NaN, which is a hole in the data and not a regime.

classes.name: RegimeCoverage
classes.doc: How many samples each regime has, and which ones the dataset does not reach at all.

methods.name: missing
methods.doc: Regimes with no sample: the dataset cannot say anything about them.

methods.name: thin
methods.doc: Regimes with fewer than ``min_count`` samples: present, but not enough to learn from.

methods.name: status
methods.doc: ``fail`` for a regime the data never reaches, ``warn`` for one it barely reaches, ``pass`` otherwise.

methods.name: missing_regions
methods.doc: The empty bands as intervals to sample in: ``{"column", "low", "high", "label"}``, ready for a sampler.

functions.name: regime_coverage
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float], spec: RegimeSpec, *, min_count: int = MIN_COUNT) -> RegimeCoverage
functions.doc: Count the samples of ``values`` in each band of ``spec``.

functions.name: regime_audit
functions.sig: (columns: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]], specs: Sequence[RegimeSpec | str], *, min_count: int = MIN_COUNT) -> list[RegimeCoverage]
functions.doc: Coverage for each spec, over the columns given. A spec whose column is absent is reported, not skipped.

children.summary: Which physical regimes a dataset covers, and which ones it is missing (#171).

children.name: pinneapple_data.registry
children.doc:
One registry for the public physics datasets and the pre-trained models (#528).

Two catalogues already existed and answered different questions: :mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.catalog` lists the
*external* public datasets (licence, whether the licence was verified, citation, homepage, the adapter that reads it)
and :mod:`pinneapple_hub.zoo` lists PINNeAPPle's own published artifacts (weights, SHA-256, version, Hugging Face
repo, model card). Each solved "how do I get this" its own way. This module is the single door in front of both:

    >>> from pinneapple_data import registry
    >>> [e.id for e in registry.list(domain="CFD")][:3]
    >>> registry.licence("flowbench")                  # printed before anything is downloaded
    >>> data = registry.load("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6", split="test")     # zoo dataset, verified SHA-256
    >>> registry.load("pdebench")                      # NoReaderError: the call that does work, named
    >>> registry.metadata("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6")    # what a run records about the data it used

It **composes, it does not re-describe**: nothing here carries its own copy of a licence, a citation or a checksum.
An entry's fields are read from the two sources at load time (``catalog.CATALOG`` and the zoo's ``manifest.json``),
so correcting the licence in one place corrects the registry, the docs table and every run record together.

The licence is shown **before** the download and the entry says whether a product may use the data: a non-commercial
licence (FlowBench's CC-BY-NC-4.0) and an access that needs registration are flagged on the entry, never discovered
after the files are on disk. The citation is printed after the load and returned by :func:`metadata`, which is the
dict a Lab run stores in its dataset card (:func:`record`).

What it will not do: invent a reader. ``airfrans`` is registered with its licence and citation and *no* loader --
the entry names the formats and the homepage, and :func:`load` raises :class:`NoReaderError` with the call that does
work today, because a registry that pretends to read ten datasets is a reading list (the argument of
:mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.catalog`). Publishing to the Hub or to Zenodo (:func:`publish`) is declared, not
executed: it needs a token and an upload the CI cannot make, and the zoo already ships its own publisher.

Command line::

    python -m pinneapple_data.registry                       # every entry, one line each
    python -m pinneapple_data.registry --docs docs/core_concepts/datasets_and_models.md
    python -m pinneapple_data.registry --licence flowbench --citation flowbench
    python -m pinneapple_data.registry --json > registry.json

classes.name: RegistryError
classes.doc: The registry cannot answer: an unknown id, or a source that does not read.

classes.name: NoReaderError
classes.doc: The entry is registered (with its licence and citation) but this library has no reader for it.

classes.name: PublishError
classes.doc: Publishing needs credentials and an upload; it is declared here and executed by the zoo's publisher.

classes.name: Entry
classes.doc: One dataset or model: what it is, who may use it, how it is cited, and whether this library reads it.

methods.name: product_warning
methods.doc: Why a product may not ship this data, in one line; empty when nothing is known against it.

functions.name: entries
functions.doc: Every entry of both sources, the external datasets first, then the zoo's own. Cached until ``reload``.

functions.name: sources
functions.doc: The problems met while reading the sources, so a caller can see a catalogue that silently went empty.

functions.name: list
functions.sig: (domain: str | None = None, kind: str | None = None, *, commercial_only: bool = False, readable: bool | None = None, source: str | None = None) -> list[Entry]
functions.doc: The entries, filtered: ``domain`` is a case-insensitive substring, ``kind`` is ``dataset`` or ``model``.

functions.name: get
functions.doc: One entry by id.

functions.name: info
functions.doc: The entry as a JSON-ready dict.

functions.name: licence
functions.doc:
The banner shown **before** the download: what the licence is, whether a product may use it, and where to
read the terms. One line, because it is printed.

functions.name: citation
functions.doc: The citation to use, or a sentence saying it is not recorded (never a guessed one).

functions.name: metadata
functions.doc:
What a run records about the data or the model it used: id, licence, citation, version and checksums.

This is the dict :func:`record` writes into a Lab dataset card and the one a report can quote; ``extra`` is
merged last, so a caller may add its own split, seed or row count.

functions.name: load
functions.sig: (entry_id: str, split: str | None = None, *, quiet: bool = False, offline: bool | None = None, **kw)
functions.doc:
Load an entry, with the licence printed before the download and the citation after it.

``split`` is passed to the zoo's dataset loader (``None`` loads every split as ``{name: split}``). A gated entry
is refused unless the caller says it has access (``allow_gated=True``), which is the point of flagging it: the
terms are somebody else's, and this module will not pretend it accepted them.

functions.name: record
functions.sig: (ctx: Any, entry_id: str, name: str | None = None, **extra) -> Any
functions.doc:
Register the use of an entry in a Lab run: the dataset card carries the licence and the citation.

    with experiment("my_study") as ex:
        data = registry.load("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6", split="test")
        registry.record(ex.ctx, "airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6")

The card's ``license`` field and its ``provenance.registry`` block are what the curation reads; nothing is
written when the entry does not exist, so a typo fails here instead of in a report six months later.

functions.name: publish
functions.sig: (entry_id: str, *, target: str = 'hub', token: str | None = None, **_) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Declared, not executed (#528): pushing a dataset or a surrogate to the Hub or to Zenodo.

The plan is returned so a caller sees exactly what would be uploaded (every file with its SHA-256, the model
card, the licence), and :class:`PublishError` says what is missing to do it. The zoo already ships the publisher
it was built with (``pinneapple_hub.zoo.publish``); this function exists so the registry has one place that says
where a published artifact comes from, instead of a fourth downloader with its own conventions.

functions.name: table
functions.doc: The entries as table cells, for the generated docs page (and for a terminal).

functions.name: to_markdown
functions.doc: The generated documentation page: the table, the legend and where each fact comes from.

children.summary: One registry for the public physics datasets and the pre-trained models (#528).

children.name: pinneapple_data.review
children.doc:
The engineering review record: a person looked at the evidence and said so (#1493, part of #1497).

Automated checks answer *is this data well formed*; they cannot answer *is this data right for the engineering
question*, because that is a judgement about the regime, the assumptions behind a boundary condition, and where the
answer is used. So approval is a **record**, not a flag:

* it names a **reviewer** and a **decision** -- there is no default and no auto-approve path, and nothing about the
  metrics can produce the reviewer;
* it is tied to the **evidence** it was given (the dataset digest and the digests of the reports), so approving one
  version of a dataset does not approve the next one;
* an exception has to name **which findings** it overrides, each with a reason -- "accept" without saying what it
  accepts is how a critical check disappears from a project;
* the store is **append-only and chained**: every record carries the digest of the previous one, so an edited or
  removed record is detected by :meth:`ReviewStore.verify` instead of being silently trusted.

The vocabulary is the one the repository already uses for operational evidence (``reviewer``, ``reviewed_at``,
``environment`` in ``pinneapple_llm/qa/levels.py``) rather than a second one.

>>> store = ReviewStore("/tmp/reviews.jsonl")                    # doctest: +SKIP
>>> rec = ReviewRecord(subject="sha256:ab...", decision="accept_exception", reviewer="A. Ribeiro",
...                    scope=[{"finding": "boundary_conditions.missing", "reason": "wall measured in test 42"}])
>>> store.save(rec).id[:12]                                      # doctest: +SKIP
'3f9c0a1b2d4e'

classes.name: ReviewError
classes.doc: The record cannot be built or saved: a missing reviewer, an unscoped exception, a broken chain.

classes.name: ReviewRecord
classes.doc:
One decision about one subject, with the evidence that was in front of the reviewer.

``subject`` is the digest of what is reviewed (a dataset digest from :mod:`pinneapple_data.readiness`, a model id
or a study reference). ``scope`` is required for ``accept_exception`` and must name findings; ``annotations``
marks regions, fields or results as ``acceptable`` / ``suspect`` / ``incorrect``.

methods.name: overridden
methods.doc: The finding ids this record accepts.

methods.name: applies_to
methods.doc: A record applies only to the evidence it was made against.

methods.name: accepts
methods.doc: Which of ``finding_ids`` this record covers -- empty when it covers none of them.

classes.name: ReviewStore
classes.doc:
Append-only, chained store of :class:`ReviewRecord` on disk (one JSON object per line).

Append-only means an edit is not offered: a new decision supersedes the old one and both stay readable. The chain
makes the edit visible anyway -- every record holds the digest of the record before it, and
:meth:`verify` recomputes the whole chain.

methods.name: save
methods.doc: Append the record. Saving the same decision twice is idempotent; it is never an edit.

methods.name: verify
methods.doc: Every problem with the chain. An empty list means the records are exactly the ones that were written.

functions.name: digest_of
functions.doc: ``sha256:`` digest of a canonical JSON dump -- the same convention the rest of the library uses.

functions.name: approval_for
functions.sig: (store: Optional[ReviewStore], subject: str, finding_ids: Sequence[str], *, required: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The review that lets ``finding_ids`` through for ``subject``, or a refusal.

Returns ``{"approved": bool, "record": id | None, "reviewer": ..., "accepted": [...], "missing": [...]}``; the gate
in :func:`pinneapple_data.readiness.require` turns it into an exception.

children.name: pinneapple_data.schema
pinneapple_data.schema.bundle
children.doc:
``PhysicsDataBundle``: a manifest and the arrays it references, as a directory on disk.

Layout of a saved bundle::

    burgers.ppb/
        bundle.json      the BundleManifest (schema pinneapple.physics-data/1), digest included
        arrays.npz       one array per key the manifest references

``bundle.json`` is indented and sorted so it diffs and reads well; ``arrays.npz`` holds one ``.npy`` per key. Both
are written with fixed timestamps, so saving the same bundle twice produces the same bytes -- a digest is only
useful if the bytes behind it are reproducible. The digest is the SHA-256 of the canonical manifest plus, in sorted
key order, the SHA-256 of every array's bytes; :meth:`PhysicsDataBundle.load` recomputes it and refuses a bundle that
does not match, which is what turns "the file says it passed" into "the file is the one that was checked".

Why a directory and not a single file: a bundle is meant to be read by other tools (h5py, xarray, ParaView), and
keeping the manifest as plain JSON is what lets them read the metadata without this library. A single ``.zip``
is available through :meth:`PhysicsDataBundle.pack` for shipping.

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_data.schema import PhysicsDataBundle, Field, AxisSpec, Physics
    >>> u = np.zeros((8, 16))
    >>> b = PhysicsDataBundle.from_arrays(
    ...     {"field:u": u, "axis:t": np.linspace(0, 1, 8), "axis:x": np.linspace(0, 1, 16)},
    ...     fields=[Field.from_array("u", u, unit="m/s", axes=("t", "x"))],
    ...     axes=[AxisSpec("t", "s"), AxisSpec("x", "m")],
    ...     physics=Physics(governing="u_t = 0"),
    ...     source="a zero field")
    >>> b.arrays["field:u"].shape
    (8, 16)

classes.name: PhysicsDataBundle
classes.doc:
A physics dataset: its manifest and the arrays the manifest points at.

The arrays are held in memory (``dict[str, np.ndarray]``, keyed exactly as the manifest's ``ArrayRef.key``)
so a caller can slice and pass them straight to a trainer. A bundle is immutable in spirit -- mutating
``arrays`` after ``save()`` invalidates the digest, and :meth:`verify` says so.

methods.sig: (arrays: Mapping[str, np.ndarray], *, fields: Sequence[Field] = (), axes: Sequence[AxisSpec] = (), physics: Physics | None = None, source: str, license: str = 'unknown', title: str = '', id: str | None = None, mesh: Mesh | None = None, geometry: Geometry | None = None, verification: Verification | None = None, inputs: Sequence[FileRef] = (), adapter: str = '', adapter_version: str = '', kind: s...

methods.doc: The values of a declared field, by its name (not its storage key).

methods.name: n_samples
methods.doc: Number of samples along the leading axis (the same length as ``t`` when there is one).

methods.doc: Record a check result, returning the (already appended) :class:`CheckResult`.

methods.name: digest

methods.name: verify

methods.doc: Read a bundle back. With ``verify_digest`` a manifest whose digest no longer matches is refused.

methods.doc: The bundle (or one field) as an ``xarray.Dataset``/``DataArray`` with its coordinates and units.

methods.name: summary
methods.doc: A one-screen description: axes, fields, units, count and provenance.

functions.doc: Module-level shortcut for :meth:`PhysicsDataBundle.save`.

children.name: pinneapple_data.schema.cae
children.doc:
CAE ⇄ bundle: what a solver wrote becomes a ``PhysicsDataBundle``, and a bundle leaves as VTU.

Every solver this repository drives already produces a neutral :class:`pinneapple_data.cae.model.Mesh` -- an OpenFOAM
case through ``cae.foam``, a CalculiX ``.frd``, an Abaqus deck, a VTU, a Gmsh mesh, a point table with fields. Until
now that mesh could be inspected, checked and rendered, but it could not become *data*: it had no licence, no
provenance, no declared unit per field and no record of what was checked. This module closes that loop in both
directions:

``bundle_from_mesh``
    a CAE ``Mesh`` plus the licence and the source becomes a bundle: nodes and **mixed** cell blocks (a volume of
    hexahedra or tetrahedra beside a surface of triangles is the normal case, and the boundary must not be dropped
    to fit a single connectivity array), the point fields as ``nodal`` and the cell fields as ``cell`` with the unit
    each one already carries, the named groups (patches, ELSETs, face zones) as ``physical_groups``, and the
    solver, format and time step as provenance.
``bundle_to_mesh``
    the inverse, so a bundle goes back through the CAE tools that read a ``Mesh`` -- quality metrics, the VTU/HDF5/
    Parquet exporters in :mod:`pinneapple_data.cae.dataset`, the 3-D views.
``export_bundle``
    one call to write a bundle as VTU (the binary XML the existing writer produces), HDF5, NPZ, Parquet, CSV, JSON
    or the PINNeAPPle UPD archive, using the exporters that already exist rather than a second copy of them.

What is deliberately *not* invented: the licence. A solver output has whatever licence its case does, and this
module asks for it instead of writing ``unknown`` into a file somebody will redistribute.

    >>> from pinneapple_data.schema.cae import bundle_from_mesh, export_bundle
    >>> bundle = bundle_from_mesh(mesh, source="CalculiX cantilever, step 1", license="CC BY 4.0")
    >>> export_bundle(bundle, "cantilever.vtu")          # the same field data the solver wrote

functions.name: bundle_from_mesh
functions.sig: (mesh: Mesh, *, source: str, license: str, title: str = '', kind: str = 'simulation', inputs: Sequence[str] = (), citation: str = '', url: str = '', notes: str = '', units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, geometry_units: str | None = None) -> PhysicsDataBundle
functions.doc:
A CAE ``Mesh`` as a :class:`PhysicsDataBundle`.

``units`` overrides the unit per field (``{"DISP": "mm", "STRESS": "MPa"}``): a CalculiX deck stores results in
the deck's own system, and the reader can only report "model units", which the schema records as ``unknown``
rather than as dimensionless. With the override the bundle passes the ``units`` gate; without it, that gate
fails and says which fields nobody declared -- a verdict the reviewer needs, not a conversion invented here.
A unit this library cannot parse is always a hard error.

functions.name: bundle_to_mesh
functions.doc: The CAE ``Mesh`` a bundle describes (unstructured bundles only), for the CAE tools downstream.

functions.name: bundle_from_files
functions.sig: (files: Mapping[str, bytes], *, source: str, license: str, **kwargs) -> PhysicsDataBundle
functions.doc: Read an uploaded CAE case (a dict of path -> bytes, as the API receives it) into a bundle.

functions.name: bundle_from_path
functions.sig: (path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, license: str, source: str = '', **kwargs) -> PhysicsDataBundle
functions.doc: Read one file or a folder (an OpenFOAM case directory) from disk into a bundle.

functions.name: export_bundle
functions.sig: (bundle: PhysicsDataBundle, path: str | os.PathLike[str], fmt: str = 'vtu') -> Path
functions.doc: Write ``bundle`` as VTU (binary XML), HDF5, NPZ, Parquet, CSV, JSON or the UPD archive.
